_note: Shared lessons as data: what one game found that another game will need, when no card or doc has room for it or it fits none. A lesson in games/<game>.md is tagged `[kb <id>]` (docs/LEARNING.md 3) and the entry is written here in the same change. No size budget: nobody reads this file end to end. `python tools/knowledge.py lessons WORD ...` searches it and every game's own lessons; `lessons --game GAME` lists the entries that apply. Fields: `id` lesson.<name> (unique); `title`; `text` (the lesson, with its limit); `level` observed | inferred | demonstrated; `sources` (games/<game>.md files that found it: add a game when it meets the lesson again), or, when no game file holds it, `origin` notes | sessions (maintainers' notes / working sessions); `words` (search terms a new game would use); optional `when` (predicates of docs/techniques/predicates.json: the entry applies unless one is known false; empty = every game) and `card` (the card it belongs with, to fold in when that card is next revised). tools/knowledge.py check validates the structure, never the truth.

lessons.title: NEXLOAD overwrites the printer buffer before the game starts
lessons.text: NEXLOAD leaves its own data in 0x5B00-0x5BFF. A snapshot that keeps its stack, code or a flag there (128K: the ROM paging code at 0x5B00 and BANKM 0x5B5C) starts wrong unless the build restores it: `keep_printer_buffer` in the converter, or a set-up call in the stub. Restore the whole 256 bytes, not only the start-up tail, and do not widen an allocation proved for part of the buffer. Boot every build with nexload=True before calling its start safe. Limit: a read of 0x5B5C alone did not matter in Atom Ant or Ruff and Reddy (real loader, every mode); check what the game does with the byte. See BRIEFING C2 #36, #38.

lessons.title: A JNext memory dump is physical SRAM, not CPU memory
lessons.text: JNext's mem/ram.bin has a 0x40000 physical offset before ordinary Next RAM, and bank 5 is dedicated video RAM. Rebuild what the CPU sees through the MMU registers, never from raw file offsets. Assert a known signature (the hook code) before reading state from a page: an all-zero count at every checkpoint was the wrong offset, not an empty table. CSpect has the same trap: its physical memory reads for the first 128K pages do not match the CPU view. A check that R-Type never touched bank 7 during level 3 read the wrong memory and gave a false assurance; it was redone by mapping the page into the CPU's address space, which showed no writes to the tile area for 150 steps. Use CPU-view reads when verifying what a game does to a bank.

lessons.title: JNext drops key presses made before the .nex has loaded
lessons.text: Loading a .nex in JNext clears earlier key presses. Schedule a run's keys after the load and confirm from the game's own state that they arrived; otherwise a run labelled moving or firing measured a neutral-input game. Besides dropping keys before the .nex loads, scripted typing into Inferno's console in JNext lost letters in the full game and a sampled screenshot often caught the wrong screen; when a command-typing test fails, retry with slower input or confirm in another way before blaming the patch (a dropped-letter script also hid a restart bug the user's exact key sequence reproduced).

lessons.title: Copy results out of a pooled simulator before the slot is reused
lessons.text: A simulator from simpool.machine is reused by the next call on the same slot. Keeping a reference to it instead of copying the result registers and memory made two different outcomes compare equal. Slots are shared by name: an original and a patched run on the same slot name reset each other and gave a false 'memory differs' (Nemesis the Warlock); runs that must coexist need different slot names.

lessons.title: The plain .nex is not the pace control for a game that beeps through the ROM
lessons.text: The plain .nex runs NextZXOS's ROM3, whose BEEP ran 12% faster than Sinclair's in JNext. A game that makes sound through the ROM needs the original .z80 on a 48K machine as its pace control. More generally the plain .nex may run NextZXOS ROM3 and so not be the faithful original baseline: a difference between plain and build at a low-memory read was the plain .nex running NextZXOS's ROM3 while the build had Sinclair's bytes (Jetpac), so check which arm is faithful first; Knight Lore needs R to match at player updates including the bootstrap and hidden ROM; Lunar Jetman's verify needs NextZXOS's ROM3 staged as a record input rather than modelling Sinclair's ROM.

lessons.title: A pace window's own overhead at 28 MHz is multiplied by K
lessons.text: The time a pace window spends on itself at 28 MHz is scaled by K like everything else in it. Account it as debt, or the target grows with every window. Seen in several forms: a nested debt reading at each of up to six plots added about a line of error each (Ruff and Reddy, fixed by one reading at the end of the pass); a window reading that holds the hook's own time, which K would scale (Renegade, 0.5 ms each); about 100 nested hooks in a scroll strip added 2% unless counted as a constant (Quazatron); broad timer windows that counted wrapper work as original time regressed pace (R-Type).

lessons.title: Check what a limiter can repay against the worst update, and read the debt's clamp first
lessons.text: A limiter that only waits cannot repay a debt larger than its window (Nightshade: 240 lines of blit against 560 of hooks). When a pace table shows a slow stretch, look at the debt's clamp before anything else: Atic Atac's clamp of -192 lines threw away most of what room changes cost, and read as 'the limiter cannot repay'.

lessons.title: Catch-up credit must be measurable, and is worth more at 28 MHz than its line count
lessons.text: Credit a catch-up gap by line count only when the gap is under a frame, and end it before any longer stretch. Run the catch-up clock as low as the build allows: at 28 MHz a gap's real gain was 3 to 8 times its lines (hooks in it against contended writes), at 7 MHz near 2 whatever it holds, so a fixed credit stays honest only there. A clock read once a frame or less often loses frames silently: count the worst case of every long hook (Nightshade Enhanced's figures took 582 lines before the first tick).

lessons.title: One floor per update cannot pace a game whose displaced work varies by figure
lessons.text: A single floor reads slow where the original is light and fast where it is busy, and the whole-run figure hides both. Windows on what was displaced, sized from the plain build, held nearly every stretch within 2%. A window that reads line and frame serial needs the two in step at the wrap (a mismatch read as 164 lines of false time per interrupt); a window under a frame needs only the wrap. The same line-plus-frame-serial mismatch at the wrap was seen in Nodes of Yesod, where it read as 164 lines of false time per interrupt and drove the account to its floor. Silkworm: with K alone, updates with many figures ran +10% and quiet ones -3%, since a window scales the logic, not a per-figure cost; a fixed debt per figure plus a higher K flattened the table (whole runs within 2%).

lessons.title: A 128K snapshot may hold a 48K game running in 128 mode
lessons.text: Count 7FFD writes, AY port use, ROM reads and non-empty banks 1/3/4/6 first. Everyone's a Wally had none, so it builds from the 128K file as-is; its sprite commit and tail followed the Rainbow (128K) path. A 128K tail must also end below 0xC000.

lessons.title: A 16K game's upper RAM is free for hook code
lessons.text: Hook RAM above 0x7FFF needs no page for a 16K game; a read and write watch in the verifier stands behind that (Jetpac).

lessons.title: Add a virtual read of figure pixels only where the data shows logic depends on them
lessons.text: Screen-reading logic is the main source of behaviour change. Treasure Island's bubbles read Dizzy's pixels and Dizzy 1's falling objects land on him (472 of 736 tests), so those need a virtual read. In Fantasy World and Magicland it would be WRONG: boxes overwrite the player, so 'screen XOR undo' no longer holds and the original leaves ghost pixels. Rainbow and Chuckie Egg have no logic reading screen pixels (collision uses an attribute buffer or coordinates).

lessons.title: Any time a hook adds to a frame-locked update costs a whole frame on many updates; measure how the game paces itself before setting a budget
lessons.text: In Inferno the game finishes an update, plays its sound in the time left, then waits for the next frame interrupt (the limiter is called from inside the screen copier, which also plays the beeper, one OUT per cell), so an update lasts its work time rounded up to the next interrupt. Measured over six full recordings (449,659 frames): spare time between update end and interrupt had a median of 5.6-8.4 ms and was often under 1 ms, so adding 1 ms delayed 2-12% of updates by a frame and adding 10 ms delayed 56-81%; added time also shortens the sound effects, and the fixed 10 ms hook budget used earlier was unmeasured and wrong. Removing all validation work from the worst updates still left about 8.5-10 ms, so tuning could not meet the goal: make a hook's total added time near zero, or pad back to the original timing.

lessons.title: The alt ROM ($8C) is the preferred patch location, but it copies NextZXOS ROM3 and its spare area may be read
lessons.text: Verified on hardware (2026-09-27): the alt ROM is a write-mode copy of the ROM, read-only afterwards, switched by 7FFD bit 4 (MMU $FF shows it, IM1, font intact; $8C is 0 at NEX launch), so hooks go in the spare block 0x386E-0x3CFF, writes are ignored and it survives 7FFD writes with no DI or paging per hook. Selecting ROM3 means 1FFD bit 2 + 7FFD bit 4 (alt image 1); the stub must page itself into slot 4 because its own 1FFD/7FFD write remaps slots 6/7. The 'all $FF at 0x386E-0x3CFF' fact is true of Sinclair's 48K ROM only: the altrom strategy copies NextZXOS ROM3, which has data at 0x3B00-0x3CFF (El Capitan Trueno's 512-byte 0xFF data patch drew figures into the ULA until that range was included in the patched bytes; checked in MAME), and the boot simulator models Sinclair's ROM so cannot see this. The spare area may also be read: That Sinking Feeling's ROM calls run the calculator at 2Dxx (entries moved to free space at 3880; nextboot.rom_paths found it), NextZXOS ROM3's IM 1 handler CALLs 0x386E and its UDG print JPs 0x387E (Starquake), Target Renegade reads 9 sound bytes at 0x3500 from ROM 0, Solomon's Key copies ROM onto itself with one caller passing BC=16384, and Inferno's intro (IM 2, I=$3B) fetches its handler address from $3BFF-$3C00, so a hook written there sent the first interrupt to garbage (level builds started from snapshots never hit it; check the I register and vector address of every phase a build can start from). A game that reads the alt ROM as data pays for every library byte there, the library can assemble anywhere a hook has mapped (Smash TV), and the ROM path check on a build with no alt ROM image reported 192-231 differing ROM3 bytes (Nightshade).

lessons.title: Archive POKs and trainers cannot be imported blindly: check against the disassembly, translate and test per release
lessons.text: Archive POKs often name addresses of another release or of the packed snapshot (Renegade, Pyjamarama: Lives and Energy addresses do not fit; Flying Shark: one address is in the packed snapshot and the rest are overwritten by the unpack, so translate through the stream map; Gryzor: the [L1] lines were data or mid-instruction; Beyond the Ice Palace: match instructions and control flow first). They can turn an opcode into a new instruction over the next bytes (Scooby-Doo 29479), freeze the game (Sabre Wulf: of 16 trainers See Ending and Paralyzed Enemies freeze it, Immunity still loses lives), use a RET trick that truncated BCD carry (Gunfright) or let an ammo index overwrite live code, have overlapping immunity variants (Highway Encounter), consume saved HL as a return address (Martianoids), poke a graphics pointer as well (Cobra: use a single poke), or only skip a bonus (Cisco Heat No Time Bonus). Head Over Heels' runtime pokes vanished at new-game reset, Dizzy Ultimate's value 256 asks for user input (omit it, and confirm the lives address by the actual DEC A), and a TOSEC dump may itself carry a POKE (Prince of the Yolkfolk 0x78AB = 0xB6): diff dumps first. Live addresses are not relocated through an original loader (generic import-pok does not): translate to the game's own data, simulate each POKE, emit a checked POK from the engine and test the complete menu-to-play path on both the patched NEX and the fix-off original snapshot.

lessons.title: Ask early for other versions of the game
lessons.text: On Inferno the PC remaster's data and screens supplied the English text, a shop reference and proof that restart could be instant, but arrived only on day five. Ask the owner early whether other versions of the game exist.

lessons.title: asm2profile reads SAVEBIN names from the top-level source file only; do not put a code entry at address 0000
lessons.text: asm2profile.assemble collects output names only from the top-level source file, so a SAVEBIN inside an included file is silently ignored. Chase H.Q.: with one shared source for three sets, the set sources carry their own SAVEBIN lines because the shared source's SAVEBINs are guarded off; separately assembled units match one source with a MODULE each, if each SAVEBIN comes before the next unit reuses its addresses. Separately, R-Type's tests break at address 0000 of a page to catch a reset, so a glide entry point at 0000 tripped it and was first misread as a crash.

lessons.title: auto names a hook build NAME_sprites.nex, and the patch command only looks for that name
lessons.text: When the default is a hook build, auto names it NAME_sprites.nex (and a loading variant NAME_sprites_loading.nex), which nxcout packages as the default; the plain conversion would be NAME.nex (Comando Quatro, Father Christmas, Flying Shark). Alien 8's nexclash patch command ends 'not supported yet' with no .nxc because userflow looks for NAME_sprites.nex and that engine writes NAME.nex and NAME_enhanced.nex (BRIEFING C2 #47 backlog); before promising an NXC release, check the engine's output name matches.

lessons.title: The automatic recorder's parts cannot be joined
lessons.text: The toolkit's recorder writes automatic recordings in parts from reloaded states; the replay loses sync at the first part's end and parts cannot be joined (each starts from another state). An explorer that plays on from the current state gives one part that replays (Olli and Lissa 3).

lessons.title: Engine detectors must read the snapshot class that auto passes
lessons.text: Army Moves and Game Over first read `.banks`, which only the converter's snapshot class has, so auto's skoolkit snapshot never matched; detect on `.memory` for that class. Atom Ant: a 128K engine's `is_` must also read skoolkit's Snapshot (`memory.banks`), the form `nexclash.py auto` passes, or auto stays on the generic path.

lessons.title: A 128K tape multiload game can be built into one .nex with every stage in Next memory; check engine code per stage
lessons.text: Cisco Heat loads each stage from tape, with scenery and sprite data differing per stage, yet all six recordings used the same interrupt handler, screen-copy routine and back buffer, so one engine covered all stages. The converted .nex carries every stage in memory with no tape. A game that resets its screen page flip between snapshots may start with either the normal or shadow screen showing, so do not assume the first snapshot's displayed screen.

lessons.title: Commit sprites after the pixel copy in back-buffer games, and hide them while a screen is copied
lessons.text: Everyone's a Wally copies the back buffer with unrolled LDI, which takes about a frame; committing sprites at the start of the blit shows them before the pixels arrive, so the commit goes after the copy (47637). Trueno hides sprites for the whole screen-change copy because old sprites flashed over the new screen.

lessons.title: With a back buffer, match the displayed frame and keep what was last shown after a partial copy
lessons.text: Bruce Lee: hardware sprite positions belong after the visible copy, not the next back-buffer plot (match the displayed frame, not the newest logical position). A figure newly drawn outside its dirty rectangle must retain its last displayed image after a full copy: hiding it produced 43 incorrect screens, retaining it closed all 5,438 comparisons. A separate tile writer (lantern restoration) was found by a single-address write trace.

lessons.title: ULA contention changes beeper edge durations even with equal instructions and R
lessons.text: Even with original clock and instruction/R parity, contention phase changes edge durations. Bound the actual I/O plus stack accesses, keep a contention-disabled diagnostic, and never claim normal waveforms byte-identical (Gunfright). Head Over Heels: AY channels A/B matched while asynchronous channel C effects differed, so equal write rates are not sound proof; report the distinction.

lessons.title: Bisect a stalled build with stripped variants and drive JNext headless
lessons.text: When Inferno's full-game build stalled, a loader-only build (no hooks) reached the menu and a build with the installer redirect disabled still stalled, which ruled out the installer in two runs. Then scripting JNext in headless mode (--headless --script, via the toolkit's jnext module) with screenshots and PC reads found the cause in a few runs. A static listing of memory shows only what is there, not whether it runs, and the simulator played the intro music that JNext and the Next did not, so the simulator can diverge on boot.

lessons.title: Measured blitter and DMA speeds: constant fill wins, per-row jobs and dithered fills do not
lessons.text: Castle Master, 192 x 64 block at 28 MHz (CSpect 4.5.9): LDIR 146 video lines, classic DMA 45 to 54, blitter 2D copy 34 to 41, CPU PUSH fill 38, blitter constant fill 14 to 21 (about 2.7 times the CPU). On hardware (matching CSpect) a 21,504-byte view copy took 143 lines by LDIR, 54 by classic DMA 3-cycle (45 at 2-cycle), 41 by blitter 2D copy (34 at 2-cycle); PUSH fill 38, blitter fill 20 (14 at 2-cycle). Starting a DMA job costs about 26 us (about a row's fill, as much as the CPU needs for 55 to 130 pixels), so one job per row loses, though re-armed short fills were cheap; a constant fill cannot write a dither pattern, and a copy from a pattern row was no faster than the PUSH fill. The 2D mode skips unused bytes between rows, beating a classic DMA copy by about a third, and needs core 3.03+; for Castle Master the blitter gained only about 0.5% of an update over the classic DMA copy, since it moves finished pixels, not polygons.

lessons.title: A build input that is not a recording has no home in the record
lessons.text: Game data a build reads (a tape's screen) has no input kind in a record: it is listed with the recordings (md5-checked, staged beside the snapshot) and the engine finds it by name (Rambo, Starquake). Tape-reading games: snapshot = the emulator start state, tapes = alternative sets, `auto --tape`; every set must rebuild the same outputs; an engine finds blocks by content as .tap and .tzx number them differently; `auto` makes no .nxc for a tape-set build and nothing yet checks the start state came from the tapes (New Zealand Story).

lessons.title: Pattern caches: key on everything the pattern depends on, compare full bytes, size by reuse analysis, and keep spare slots
lessons.text: Hashes or checksums only narrow the search: compare bytes on every hit (Knight Lore; Ghosts n Goblins: the checksum only indexes the store on a miss, since checksum plus linear walks cost 3x the lookup: hook T -42%, pace +6.56% -> -0.00%). Key on the whole input (Rainbow: IX, start row, AF' carry, the whole graphics stream) so rewritten graphics at the same address cannot go stale, but keep the vertical phase out of the key (put it in the sprite Y) or every scroll step misses; still run the plotter once on a hit for the register state, and colour by graphics page only works for fixed addresses. Cache by image address across figures (Herbert: per-slot caches can pass pixels while rebuilding one animation many times); zero mono cache bytes do not prove hardware patterns are initialised, so initialise every used opaque-black pattern in setup (Gunfright). Size from a reuse analysis first (Rainbow: 32 LRU entries 63%, 64: 83%, a 256K store in Next RAM pages 32-63 at MMU1 91-94%; Lunar Jetman simulating on the hook call log: per-slot tile cache saved 60% of uploads, content-shared pool 97%). Policy: on a miss replace the group unused longest (Ghosts n Goblins level-3 pace +0.93 -> +0.56%), size uploads to the shape shown (half were half empty), deduplicate packed parts and mirrored forms and keep 12 spare slots (Bruce Lee), six spare patterns suffice for four-part figures and prepare all parts before one attribute burst (Exolon).

lessons.title: Tell figures apart through a shared routine by the caller's return address
lessons.text: When one plotter draws several kinds of figure, read the return address on the stack at the plotter entry (Chuckie Egg 39500: the call from 41238/41361 means the duck, else the player), a register the routine pushed (the hen plotter's caller DE = hen table entry), or IY for routines that end JP (IY) (Rainbow: cell composition vs spawning into a drawn cell). No hook state is needed.

lessons.title: A cell-map renderer has no pixel-level attribute clash
lessons.text: Trap Door (48K) keeps two cell maps of tile set, tile index and attribute (32 x 20 cells), composes objects into the current map, diffs it against the previous map and copies only the changed cells to the screen; figures move in whole 8x8 cells, so there is no classic pixel attribute clash and the visible fault is a figure's cell hiding everything behind it (square cut-outs). This was read from a disassembly and survey counts, not proven by a probe, and led to the game being logged as analysed and skipped; no tool says there is no colour clash to remove (an attribute-change count cannot tell a cell copier from clash), so a process step that flags this before design work would save effort. Suggested Next design: ULA shows what is underneath, a 1-bit text-mode tilemap shows the top object, with the limits of no mirror bit and 512 tiles.

lessons.title: When the loop budget is the problem, make the loop cheaper before tuning repayment
lessons.text: Tuning how overage was repaid only moved the miss around (+7% slow stretches, -33% bursts); compiling known sprites to code removed the overage and windows came within a few percent both ways (Jilly's Farm). Highway Encounter likewise: do not tune a limiter to conceal real cost; retain the measured failure.

lessons.title: Check patch sites for writes during play; model the operation byte in force
lessons.text: Games self-modify: the Treasure Island title ISR writes 63340; Magicland's object plotter rewrites its own operation byte (NOP / XOR (HL)) and a JP into a mirror path; Rainbow has self-modified operands at 59522, 59565, 59085 that must stay out of signatures and patch sites. Run an analysis for writes to any intended patch site and model the op that is currently in force.

lessons.title: Check the video refresh setting before chasing a 'plays too fast' report; measure the original's frames-per-update distribution
lessons.text: The owner's report that R-Type played fast was a 60 Hz mode toggled in error, not a pacing fault; the core and video mode (50 or 60 Hz) are worth asking for with any hardware speed report. Measure the original's frames-per-update distribution before choosing a pace: R-Type's original averaged 4.35 frames per update (28% at 3, 34% at 4, 22% at 5), its title alternated 2 and 3 frames and level 2 contained updates of 5 frames; the owner accepted dropping the original's slowdown and holding a steady 4 frames per update, with equivalence extremely close, not exact.

lessons.title: Measure the write extent of every dispatch target, not just those the recording reaches
lessons.text: Run each original plotter entry from a mid-screen address and record the columns and rows it writes. Rainbow's 4-wide leftward entries write E-3 while the sprite window started at E-2; the boss spider lost a column on hardware although both RZX were IDENTICAL, because only the boss uses those entries. A hardware video of the fault ('left column missing only when facing left') was enough to point at the mirrored entries when no RZX existed. Also measure 'once per frame' claims: the walker ran up to 14 times per render.

lessons.title: Colour from the cell under a sprite is clash moved to the sprite layer
lessons.text: Check by layer before trusting a clash report's cause (Three Weeks; two-plot figures show it first). A game's look can read as monochrome and still have a little clash: measure figure cells by attribute (Scooby-Doo). No tool says 'there is no colour clash to remove': an attribute-change count cannot tell a cell copier from clash (Trap Door).

lessons.title: Check for a clean copy buffer before building a composer; a game's own screen capture can be a trap
lessons.text: Altered Beast: keeping the back buffer intact and redirecting only the blit's source gave identical game memory with one small hook; this works when a clean copy exists in memory at blit time and the game reads neither buffer nor screen. Army Moves: the game captures the screen into its clean buffer at the title, so the logo came out grey until a hook put painted cells back first.

lessons.title: A clean scenery copy can come from the moment before the first plot or a reset, not a commit
lessons.text: A clean copy need not exist in the game: the moment before the first plot of a frame gives one when erases run in exact reverse order (Ikari Warriors). Freeze scenery at reset, not at commit, or copying the live clean buffer presents edits one update early (Herbert). A composite whose clean copy is captured after figures are plotted needs the plots undone first (Knight Tyme).

lessons.title: Collision often reads attributes (BRIGHT): leave background attributes alone
lessons.text: Dizzy collision tests use the attribute BRIGHT bit, so converted figures must not change the scenery's attributes. Rainbow tile collision reads its own attribute buffer; Chuckie Egg's attribute refresh from the map constantly repaints figure colour squares, so removing the paints keeps the map colours.

lessons.title: Key per-pixel colour maps by a pixel of the unshifted image, not by memory address
lessons.text: For Rainbow Islands the player's picture is moved (shifted) in memory as he walks, so keying paint by address needed a sheet copy of every frame at every shift. Keying by a pixel of the unshifted picture lets one figure per animation frame cover all shifts, so the painting sheet got much smaller with nothing lost. Painted colours are applied only when a piece is first converted and cached, so the cache key must also include the graphic's address and shift; otherwise two graphics with identical bytes share colours. Painted pieces used sprite palette 15, a pattern pixel is then a sheet colour.

lessons.title: Items drawn on the tilemap use one ink per tile, so a sprite colour map does not reach them
lessons.text: In Rainbow Islands the collectables are drawn on the tilemap in one ink per tile. Painting their sheet did nothing on the Next (only the player and thrown rainbow, 480 of 4,353 map entries, changed) until the colour map is wired into the tile builder. Transparent paint was also unsupported, so black outlines were kept. Existing unit tests expecting the old ink colours fail once a map is applied, so run them on the build without the map.

lessons.title: Colour sheet and recolour pitfalls
lessons.text: Bubbler: the importer truncated palettes at 15 entries (now the declared length); indexes above 15 must serialize as explicit integer arrays since variable-width hex loses pixel boundaries. Altered Beast: coloursheet.choose picks figures by key, so pixels under a second part are on no sheet; painting the whole-figure sheet with `recolour --layout` covers them. Cauldron: a painting read back from an older sheet replaced the whole map (kept 0 of 1,593 entries); recolour now merges, and sheets store the engine's colour_identity (refused on mismatch). An outline ring lies outside the graphic's bytes: use per-image ring keys. A colour rule from a figure's first cell carries the clash into the sprite; coloursheet.write crashes on a figure with no opaque pixel.

lessons.title: Dead registers pass a compare made at the original's return
lessons.text: A stand-in that left C wrong passed a compare at the plot's return because the next row reloads C; compare at the stand-in itself, where the register is still live.

lessons.title: Verify against the original's own frames or buffer, not only against your own model
lessons.text: A second, independent comparison with the game's real screen or buffer catches what hooks and the first model share. Abu Simbel's verify passed with figures over water and ice because the model was the author's; only frames beside the original showed the balls should sink. Altered Beast's model compared with the game's own buffer every game frame found the level-end curtain, an attribute writer outside the plotters and an 8-bit attribute address glitch; Bubbler's final front-buffer comparison caught saved rectangles, in-place flips and partial death copies that private-canvas checks missed; Army Moves' title capture trap was found only by looking at the soak sheet; Dizzy Ultimate: also check pixels touched by the ORIGINAL, since following only patched writes let a missing scenery hook escape. Silkworm's GAME OVER was missing from Layer 2 with every check passing since hooks and model shared the blind spot (text writer 5BEF); Scooby-Doo's mono model fed with the release's own bytes finds a missed writer the colour model cannot; Solomon's Key's composite check found the game's one-pass glitches; Page Pharaoh's whole-picture model caught the column-31 wrap; Pac-Mania's unit tests against the real plotter on canvases found a y ring wrap; Treasure Island: reconstruct a monochrome picture from drawing events and compare with the original bitmap before trusting a colour mock-up. Jilly's Farm hooked eight routines' callers and replay passed, yet the menu stayed all ULA because 8BE9 falls into a copy at 8BED past any CALL (comparing the model's master plane with the real screen at every copy caught it); a plane model and hook agreed and both were wrong (OR IYh has no planes on Spec256) until a frame diff against the set's own emulator; Mad Mix 2's model caught a lost MMU line, and native picture inspection caught Herbert's selector mistake and a shared menu-glyph error in Head Over Heels. Hook the routine, not its callers.

lessons.title: Compiled BASIC reads the screen through runtime PEEK/POINT/ATTR routines
lessons.text: Find those runtime routines and class reads by return address; `scan --writers` also lists readers (the card's earlier 'no shared command' was wrong). Cauldron.

lessons.title: Install hooks after the game decompresses its code, by redirecting a later call
lessons.text: Inferno's main code is compressed on the tape, so hook bytes cannot be applied to the file in advance. The BASIC loader calls USR 24200 twice (decompress, then start); redirecting the second call to a small installer that writes all hooks into the decompressed code, then starts the game, worked on real hardware once the vector fix was in. Confirm in a replay that the hook sites hold the expected bytes after decompression.

lessons.title: Confirm a cause with a trace before writing it down
lessons.text: A reset after patching C027 was first blamed on a 'game load check' and noted as 'never patch bank 0'; the real cause was a 7FFD remap. Confirm a cause with a trace (PC and MMU at the reset) before recording it (R-Type).

lessons.title: Copying an engine can silently take over the recolour guard
lessons.text: recolour.engines() takes the last own module of a record that defines RECOLOUR, so a copied engine module must drop it or it takes over the record's guard (it refused its own build, Rainbow Islands engine); a RECOLOUR registered with a map format the shared tool cannot read (Starquake, Stormbringer: the engine's own map form is not what recolour.run reads; Spellbound's first verify failed on map form) should stay unregistered or be normalised.

lessons.title: A screen copier may also play sound and limit speed: replay each beeper OUT from inside the fast routine
lessons.text: Inferno's screen copier sends one byte per screen cell to the beeper (416 per update, about half the updates change the sound) and calls the speed limiter after row 6, so the limiter's recoverable time is the first 13 rows of the copy. Running such a copier at 28 MHz garbles the sound, and replaying logged OUTs after a fast head cannot work because the first OUT is due 244 T after the start while the head takes about 5 ms. Each OUT must be played as the head reaches its cell, at the original T, timed by reading a CTC channel (32 T per tick), with the original copier as fallback if the CTC does not count; in the simulator OUT timing was within about +/-56 T, the return to the limiter within about 41 T, and a 48K contention model made the original 0.3-0.5% longer. Never install the fast head without the pad to the original return time or the game runs faster; check for OUT 254 and limiter calls inside any routine you plan to speed up or replace.

lessons.title: Read a copy routine's destination and beam timing, do not assume
lessons.text: Phantis part 1's copy pops a table of screen addresses and adds 1 before use, so work column 0 is screen column 3; the first overlay sat one column left. A copy slower than a frame stays behind the beam, so what it writes shows from the next frame's top and a flip at its end falls mid screen: split the row count and flip in the middle. Nemesis: row address arithmetic per row cost 3x the copy (620 T/row); compute the visible row range and screen address once and step with the next-line routine.

lessons.title: Check the CPU speed in load and redraw phases: a stale flag left them at 3.5 MHz
lessons.text: R-Type's level-start pause was 348 frames (about 7 s) because the run_fast flag was still 0 from the title, so every interrupt dropped the CPU to 3.5 MHz while the interrupt-driven Layer 2 clear and draw ran. Running 28 MHz throughout and making the clear a DMA fill gave 112 frames (start-key-to-play 348 to 112); a later measurement showed the remaining time was per-cell computation, not byte copying. Check what sets and resets the speed across screen transitions and on every path including the title, not only inside the play loop.

lessons.title: CSpect for live debugging, JNext for unattended scripted runs; connect the headless emulator on day one
lessons.text: CSpect (4.5.9) started with its -mcp switch opens a local control server (screenshots, registers, memory, disassembly, breakpoints on code, memory and port, single-step and step back, key presses, loading a .nex); it sometimes starts paused in its debugger and a run call releases it, and its tools only appear in a Claude Code session that starts while CSpect is already running. It has no unattended scripting, so frame-timed key presses, logs and update counts stay on JNext (frame-keyed key scripts, headless mode). The owner wants CSpect preferred when available and JNext otherwise; a fault seen in both emulators is probably the build's own. Connect headless JNext on day one: on Inferno it was connected two days after the user asked, a stall cost about 25 minutes of wrong theories and listings pasted by the user, and after connecting the cause was found in about two minutes. JNext limits: it does not emulate the blitter at all (1.3.0 included; CSpect does), and headless runs show screens, PC and memory but are silent, so sound and beeper pitch need a real Next. The toolkit's JNext notes were written for 1.1.104 while the user had 1.1.87 and 1.2.0, so check behaviour on the installed version; scripted input needs the game's own key timing (one game needed Enter after each menu key) and an idle prompt may drop into an attract demo.

lessons.title: CSpect press_keys needs held keys joined with +
lessons.text: With the CSpect control server, held keys must be written like 3+5; '35' is silently ignored. Also, CSpect cannot set R-Type's level byte at the title because the title code resets it. Snapshot-started builds had sprites off until the next life.

lessons.title: Calibrate tick-quantised constants over all CTC phases
lessons.text: Calibrate tick-quantised timing constants over all CTC phases: five phases left K 7 T off a hook in Inferno, and constants holding NEXTREG 7,x need the machine's own figure (cw_cal).

lessons.title: CTC channel 3 (prescaler 256, 32 T tick) is a polled clock for T-exact waits
lessons.text: Inferno's copier window polls CTC channel 3 as its clock: one tick is 32 T of the 3.5 MHz-equivalent clock in every video timing, so 50 Hz and 60 Hz need no change, and the 56 T tolerance used is one tick plus rounding and polling delay; if the CTC does not count, the build falls back to the original code. A raster-line timer was judged too coarse for about 1% of updates when waiting until the moment the original routine would have finished, so the CTC was used. Hooks measuring their own added time on it held the measured value within a few T of the true value in the simulator; the simulator has no ULA contention (the beeper port is contended on a 48K), so timer settings and sprite-port timing at 28 MHz still need hardware measurement.

lessons.title: zxnDDMA exists only from core 3.03.00; keep pre-3.03 measurements apart and review every new game
lessons.text: zxnDDMA (port 6B, core 3.03.00+) adds 22-bit physical SRAM addressing that bypasses the MMU and does not reach BRAM banks 5 and 7, 2D rectangle transfers with strides, and transparent or fill modes. Its guide's timings come from core 3.02.21 or an unnamed 'issue 5 at 28 MHz', not a released 3.03.00 board, and must never budget a pre-3.03 or no-blitter fallback; the 3.02.00 board measurements (including wrong copies at 3.5 MHz, fixed in 3.02.02) apply only to the classic DMA. The printed Next manual 3rd edition covers roughly core 3.01.x and has no Layer 2, sprite or DMA chapters; core register text and VHDL are the ground truth. The contribution rules ask every new game for a DMA and core 3.03.00 DDMA review with a no-blitter fallback (docs/DDMA.md); Chase H.Q. Enhanced, built on plain zxnDMA before the rule, has the review open.

lessons.title: Debug layer problems by switching Next layers off one by one
lessons.text: In MAME, switch layers off from Lua (NextReg 0x15, 0x68, 0x69, using emu.step() while paused) and read sprites from the sprite attribute RAM share: the human sees the guilty layer at once. A cover check at every copy (buffer before copy versus scenery after = the figures' pixels; each must lie under an opaque sprite pixel) found two real bugs in Trueno.

lessons.title: Do not idle for the raster before every buffer flip
lessons.text: Castle Master's renderer idled on average about 21 video lines before every flip. Letting the next view's geometry start at once and flipping from a check inside the geometry loop once the raster had left the view gave +11.8% views per update. Only the final view still waits, so the pace is untouched.

lessons.title: Delay-loop screens run too fast at 28 MHz: speed up only during play
lessons.text: R-Type's title, attract and name-entry screens time themselves with CPU delay loops and ran 8 times too fast with the main loop at 28 MHz (logo flipped to high scores too quickly, name entry unusable; pace came out at 4.35 frames per update with the title alternating 2 and 3, so a fixed 28 MHz pace of 3 ran 45% fast there). Run 3.5 MHz outside play and 28 MHz only during play: the title-to-high-score cycle was then 621 frames against the original's 597 and dying and respawning took as long as the original. Check every non-play screen for software timing when speeding up a game.

lessons.title: Default builds keep the original 16 colours; enhancements are optional
lessons.text: Project owner rule from Winter Sports: smoother, similar gameplay with the original palette takes precedence; graphics may be updated per pixel (removing attribute clash) but the original 16 colours must stay. More advanced options such as painted scenery must be user-switchable in the NXC patch, as a colour set or toggle, not the default.

lessons.title: Find figures the original draws behind scenery by replaying and counting hidden cells
lessons.text: A replay of the whole recording counting, per figure family, the updates where scenery hid some of its cells found 53 R-Type families hidden in 50+ updates (fewer than that is a brush against a wall). They were first flagged to stay in the ULA; that was later superseded by drawing everything as sprites and cutting figures with scenery masks. A first flag check never matched because it tested Z while A held a non-zero byte, and shipped before the owner's report exposed it.

lessons.title: Switch Layer 2, tilemap and sprite layers off on every non-play (ULA-drawn) screen, and back on when play resumes
lessons.text: Layer 2 scenery, tilemap and sprites cover ULA-drawn screens, and stale sprites stay on top of a new ULA picture after death, continue, round end, game over, access-code screens, pause menus, message windows, high-score and name-entry screens and screen copies (R-Type high-score table and name entry; Inferno's death menu showed only its top rows; Rainbow, Trueno, Page Pharaoh, Ruff and Reddy). Find every path that leaves play, including ones that never reach the figure plotter: Inferno's exits all passed one routine, so one hook there hides both layers (hook the instruction after the first when the first's bytes are rewritten at run time; cancel Copper-queued commits at the exit); Rainbow's stubs write NextReg $15 = 0 and the next commit sets it to 1; Trueno wraps its window routine in a stub that hides Layer 2 (NextReg 0x69) and sprites (0x15) and restores them on return (ask the human whether the game has such windows, otherwise read PC and stack while one is up); R-Type's build disables scenery and sprites as soon as the high-score check starts. The converse also matters: R-Type's continue screen turned sprites off and nothing turned them back on, so every path returning to a sprite-drawn screen must switch them on again; menus and end screens also hold their own plots (Page Pharaoh's menu icons were missing until the overlay was shown there; Ruff and Reddy's pause exit left the overlay over the title and figures stayed over LEVEL COMPLETE without a hide at D42B). Whatever was removed from the ULA is missing while the layers are off, which Trueno's owner accepted.

lessons.title: Entry-only checks miss loops that branch into displaced bytes
lessons.text: Entry-only ABI checks missed loops branching into displaced bytes (Head Over Heels): keep small whole loops in immutable trampolines or put the patch ahead of every back edge, and check original and patched routines through return. In a fast C replay an interior of a patched entry hit once means an interrupt between its first instructions (Monty is Innocent). The verifier must permit reached displaced interiors but not arbitrary interior jumps (Highway Encounter); a game may also call inside a routine (Lode Runner's gold XOR enters 0x984A, not 0x983E).

lessons.title: Skip-the-routine tests prove display-only only for the paths the recording takes; read the code too
lessons.text: A test that skips a routine (or a trace over a recording showing nothing outside the stage reads what it writes) proves it display-only on the recorded paths only; branches the recording never takes, and anything the stage patches into other code (a copier's self-modified code), stay unchecked and must be listed as such. Inferno spent about 44 hours (4.5 days) preserving every register, R value and RAM effect of the screen copier; eight minutes after the brief dropped that goal, a test that skipped the copier entirely, supplying the recorded LD A,R values, left game RAM identical on 5 of 6 levels (identical on levels 1-4 and 6 for 2,500 frames). Disassembly later found gameplay logic inside the copier (a CALL Z at 9804, ending in a jump back into the main loop) on a path the replays never reached. Use the skip test and the disassembly together; the project owner corrected a summary that had said measured, not assumed for exactly this reason.

lessons.title: A game transition drawn through a non-view path can drop the colour layer
lessons.text: On hardware, lowering the drawbridge changed the castle back to the original colours until the next move: the redraw went through the game's dissolve effect and the build treated every dissolve as a non-view screen, switching Layer 2 off. Fix: keep the dissolve, and bring colour back when it ends; the owner then asked for the dissolve itself to run in colour (new view drawn off screen and faded over the old in the game's four passes), confirmed good on hardware. The simulator proves only the end result, not how the passes look.

lessons.title: DivMMC traps: RST 38 trap, 3Dxx automatic paging region, and IM 1 reaching ROM 0x0038 once the trap is gone
lessons.text: A whole hidden ROM does not remove a delayed DivMMC RST 38 trap; clear only its enabling bit and keep the other controls (Underwurlde). Once DivMMC no longer traps RST 38, a game running IM 1 (or intro IM 2 with I=3B, whose vector is ROM 3BFF-3C00) reaches alt-ROM hook space at 0x386E / 0x0038: Jetpac executed hook code at 0x386E, Match Day's menus ran IM 1 into 0xFF bytes with RST 38 recursion, Inferno's intro vector bytes must stay FF; found by JNext headless and masked under NextZXOS. Exolon's relocated padding copy at 3D80 passed the simple model but stopped native JNext after 17 updates and ran when moved to 3600; the 3Dxx DivMMC automatic-paging region is a suspected cause and is an inference only.

lessons.title: A DMA job can swallow the frame interrupt; chunk it or fall back to the CPU near the interrupt
lessons.text: A classic zxnDMA job holds the bus, so the CPU cannot see the frame interrupt, and the simulator does not model this. Cisco Heat's 32-byte DMA screen copy lost an interrupt every few seconds in JNext (49.94 a second, one 40.5 ms gap), which can upset music and timers; the fix was to use DMA only when the copy ends 90 lines before the next interrupt (otherwise the game's own copy), and to run the pace tool after any DMA change. Castle Master's whole-view transfer lasts several milliseconds, far longer than the interrupt pulse, so it is done in chunks of 8 rows (about 458,000 T down to about 114,000 T), with LDIR instead of a chunk that could cover the interrupt line (line 248 VGA, 256 HDMI) and a CPU fall-back on cores older than 3.00 (the blitter needs 3.03.00); tested in the simulator on both interrupt lines. With hardware IM2 on, a pending interrupt can also hold a transfer back. Real-hardware timing is the real test.

lessons.title: Whole-row DMA and blitter copies are safe only in stable mapped RAM; tiny copies prefer the CPU
lessons.text: Whole-row DMA is safe only across stable mapped RAM; backward expanded-byte overlap needs grouped LDD to keep read/write order, and core and hardware-IM2 fallbacks must run the same independent oracle (Highway Encounter). Gunfright's DMA path is selected only where capability and hardware-IM2 gates allow, with CPU-only paths passing the same ABI. Inferno: tiny copies prefer CPU, charge stalls separately, and physical SRAM addresses include a 040000 aperture offset.

lessons.title: Boot and DMA models must honour real mapping
lessons.text: Boot simulation must honour the NEX entry bank: a bank-32 loading-screen wrapper was otherwise bypassed (wrapped and unwrapped game-entry states now compare equal). A virtual DMA transfer needs the game's actual mapped-memory callbacks; CPU alt-ROM reads are not proof of DMA visibility, so check source, full destination and gaps (Rainbow Islands DMA).

lessons.title: Deferred work in timed gaps: drop unfinished work at the deadline rather than finishing it late, and bound the scan
lessons.text: In Inferno, work run in a copier's wait gaps that was not finished at the deadline cost up to 24.7k T (about 7 ms) when finished late, in the 10% of updates where the beeper changes nearly every cell. Dropping it, with the display keeping the last complete frame, made the late hook a constant 156-160 T; carrying half-done work into the next window did not work because the next capture overwrites the data the work reads. Dropped updates (12-18% in the model) can chain into long stale runs, so measure the longest run and report drops, not only the rate, since every added coroutine stage raises the drop rate. A 64-slot scan per new pattern cost 2.5k T and doubled drops (a recency list fixed it); busy windows are nearly full, so per-chunk cost, not cold frames, sets the run length.

lessons.title: Apply 8-bit x wrap before clipping; test x+width after rejecting out-of-view x
lessons.text: Apply the eight-bit x wrap before clipping (255+1=0), as the original does; original-map and ULA negative controls caught a wrong 25-tick model (Inferno). Martianoids' renderer allows linear right-edge spill: clip against the 192-pixel original buffer before translating to the 256-pixel display and reject x beyond the viewport before an 8-bit x+width test can wrap.

lessons.title: Compare an Enhanced build's fixed colours as RGB, not only as symbols
lessons.text: Fixed colours were compared only as symbols, never with the RGB the set-up uploads (found by a review in Pssst and Tranz Am): replay the boot's NEXTREG writes against the painted map, with the default build as the negative. Sabre Wulf: a fixed palette entry painted on a pixel the game colours at run time (orchid bloom) hides the game's cue; give such pixels the run-time colour.

lessons.title: Owner rule: gameplay extremely close, not 1:1; name what consumes each preserved item and relax exact gates nothing reads
lessons.text: The owner changed the project rule from identical to extremely close: exact matching stays the default where cheap, but a difference the game never reads later is accepted and listed in the record with the reason. For every must-preserve, name what consumes it: Inferno's biggest delay came from an untested requirement to keep every original instruction, register, R value, RAM effect and beeper event, when R is a random source in the level code that matters only when matching a recording (skipping the copier and supplying recorded LD A,R values matched game RAM on five levels, levels 3, 4 and 6 diverged without them), so handle it in the test harness, not at run time (R can be fed from the recording during tests); state the goal as a playable, recognisable game. R-Type's checks that every register (R included) and 42,240 bytes of RAM matched at every update made the replacement too slow; asking what reads each value and dropping the rest led to the 28 MHz fix, and where R is a random source two runs with no input diverge and cannot be compared bit for bit. Inferno's strictest layers (exact R, lost-interrupt compensation) were later judged unnecessary.

lessons.title: List every caller of a plotter, not only the hooked entry
lessons.text: Before hooking, find all callers of the plotter and eraser and every writer of the undo pointer: Dizzy 6 plots a mirrored copy through the same plotter via a second call site and a switched undo buffer; Trueno's dragon energy bar enters the figure plotter past the hook (via 0x82E4). Screens with a special build (end screen, transitions) need Layer 2 and sprites cleared or hidden on each such path.

lessons.title: Exact per-cell hiding of partly covered figures cost too much; use draw order instead
lessons.text: R-Type exact per-cell hiding matched the original pixel for pixel but cost about 15 ms per update in the busiest level 2 scene (15 slow updates in 300), so it was removed. Instead a figure the game only partly draws is placed behind the whole figures, and black parts of scenery are made solid so scenery hides figures as in the original. The remaining difference is see-through overlaps where the figure behind shows through gaps in the one in front.

lessons.title: Exact per-cell hiding of partly covered figures cost about 15 ms per update
lessons.text: Building exact per-cell hiding (sprite cut where the ownership map says another figure or scenery is in front) matched the original pixel for pixel but cost about 15 ms per update in the busiest R-Type level 2 scene and caused 15 slow updates in 300, so it was dropped. The cheaper rule: put a partly drawn figure behind all whole figures, make black scenery parts solid so scenery hides figures as in the original, and let the first-drawn figure stay on top of overlapping ones. The remaining difference is a see-through look where the figure behind shows through gaps in the one in front.

lessons.title: Learn a plotter's layout and exact figure pixels by running the original on empty and full canvases
lessons.text: Run the original plotter on a canvas instead of decoding graphics: a screen or buffer of 0x00 shows the ink pixels, 0xFF shows what it clears (the mask); for an OR plotter read screen pixels as 0, for a plotter that composes background read tile graphics as 0. Single-bit graphic streams on 00 and FF screens give target byte, mirroring and mask-versus-ink for every stream byte (Rainbow Islands: test the table against the plotter on random streams plus a corrupted-table control, and keep one original plotter run per piece for the register state); an empty and a full screen gave byte order, empty rows and the mask's corner at once and the model matched at every shift (Olli and Lissa 1 and 3, where the first layout model was wrong by a row, a byte and a pixel; an unmasked figure starts a line higher than a masked one since the OR loop starts at the mask's first row, Olli and Lissa 2). Chuckie Egg's sprite pixels equalled the canvas set at every event and Trueno got an exact silhouette with no code reading; guessing the body by morphology was rejected.

lessons.title: Waiting the original routine's exact T by path beats a K ratio
lessons.text: A K window was wrong in both directions in Mad Mix 2 because the body's clock ratio differs by path (LDI heavy against register heavy). Replays give the original routines' exact T per path; waiting those out gave +0.1% against +-5% and needs no per-emulator tuning. Prefer it where the time is a simple function of the arguments.

lessons.title: Fades and black scenes need the sprites off for their length
lessons.text: A fade to black and a scene on a black screen need the sprites off for their length: figures the game drew fade or go black with the attributes, a sprite would not (Olli and Lissa 2). A list the game fills then plays gives the display switch for nothing: stage at the add, switch on at the play, and a pass that adds nothing clears the sprites, so no hook at room changes and no stale sprite (Olli and Lissa 3).

lessons.title: A routine run faster must be padded back to the original duration, or the game speeds up
lessons.text: Making a game's drawing routine cheaper makes the game run faster unless the update is padded or the saving credited back to the original timing. Inferno's fast copier (7.2-7.6 ms against 26.9-29.7 ms) must never be installed without the wait that ends when the original copier would have finished (pad time from a formula with a fitted correction, replay error about 600 T, hooks within about 120 T). Winter Sports Bobsled, Ice Hockey, Speed Skating and Biathlon plugins used frame halts plus a 28 MHz draw (Bobsled and Biathlon within 2-3% of original pace, Ice Hockey and Speed Skating about 6% fast). Cisco Heat's first sprite fast path made the game 14% faster in the simulator (bench frames per update, not only lines). Gryzor: NOPing a plotter's stores saves only 3 T a byte, less than a hook's fixed entry and exit at 3.5 MHz (about 250 T), so a 28 MHz hook in front of the loop made it slower (+3,800 T a tick) while replacing the whole loop gave +36 T a tick. Everyone's a Wally Updated and Booty: a hook that replaces a plot needs the plot's original time back in the wait, or pace still moves with plot count.

lessons.title: Use the C simulator with frame-level hooks for analysis and censuses; per-instruction Python hooks are ~100x slower
lessons.text: Replaying Trueno's 53,543-frame RZX with SkoolKit's C simulator and a patched RZXTracer.next_frame (memory checked at each frame end) takes 4-8 s; per-instruction Python hooks need many minutes (one dict scan per opcode turned a 2-minute pass into a 10-minute timeout). For a first look at an unknown engine, rzxplay --map plus sna2ctl -m plus sna2skool -c gives a routine-split disassembly of everything the RZX executed in about a minute, and rzxplay --stop N with an output .z80 at ten points gives a contact sheet. Cauldron: tools/probes/rzx_census.py counts and finds the first frame of given PCs over a 90K-frame recording in about 4 minutes with the C simulator against about an hour in Python, and a whole-RZX sheet capture through rzx.trace takes about 70 s.

lessons.title: Smooth figure motion comes from glide plus an even update rhythm, not from resolution
lessons.text: R-Type moves every figure in whole 8-pixel cells and updates about every 3 to 5 frames; sprites position in whole pixels, so smoothness comes from moving the sprite 1/P of the way each frame, P being the frames the last update took. Objects must be matched between updates (by object, graphic and order); slots are reused when an enemy dies and respawns, so big jumps (over 4 cells), flashing and new figures do not glide. Collisions stay cell-based, so a part-way sprite may look like it touches before the game counts a hit.

lessons.title: Before optimising hooks in a CPU-paced game, find where the frame is paced
lessons.text: Rainbow Islands runs its whole frame in the IM2 handler with interrupts off, one game frame per 3 interrupts (95%) or 4 (5%), with no limiter: at 7 MHz the original runs too fast. A limiter of a few instructions at handler entry plus 28 MHz for the game frame removed all slowdown and made hook cost irrelevant, while the main loop stayed at 3.5 MHz with its own timing. Measure the original pace from the RZX (frames between handler entries). Per-piece hooks and caches had not fixed the slowness on hardware (cache v1 gave no visible gain).

lessons.title: Trace first accesses with the game's periodic interrupts delivered
lessons.text: Bruce Lee: a no-interrupt lookahead stalled in the game wait loop and could not show that the byte below SP is first overwritten by the original ISR; deliver the original periodic interrupts during first-access tracing and retain every byte until its own first write is observed.

lessons.title: Remove an object from a screen the game redraws right after the game draws that part
lessons.text: Clearing sprite-converted items once at render end left the item visible between the blit and the fix (flicker). Rainbow now fixes each 8-line band at the walker end, right after the band's blit and attribute copy. An object's mask may include its own graphic bits ((cell AND mask) OR gfx with gfx inside the mask), so clear with AND (mask AND NOT gfx), or the ink pixels remain.

lessons.title: Flashing figures: convert once and flash with the sprite palette offset
lessons.text: R-Type converts flashing figures (colour override 8EB1) once in colour 1, and the sprite's palette offset picks the flash colour; sprite palette entry 16n+1 holds colour n.

lessons.title: The flicker check with a .z80 control can read zero transients
lessons.text: Cobra: with a .z80 control the original's attribute transients read 0 (its screen is not in that run's bank 5 VRAM file) although the original flashes the same cells (JNext mem[] log). The plain .nex is the control.

lessons.title: Do not put clean attributes on the visible screen after the game's copy
lessons.text: Comando Quatro: writing clean attributes after the game's copy looked safe with a beam wait, but memory at a frame boundary and the unsynchronised wipe copies still showed painted cells; never putting them on the screen is simpler than timing around them.

lessons.title: Force inputs the recording never has: the original may overflow, and the replacement must not copy it
lessons.text: Castle Master: forcing (27391) = 0 (lightning) found an original bug: at pitch 4 a 255-row bolt overwrites RAM including the face list. A renderer drawing into its own pages must not copy that; make it a model option (bolt clipped) and record it.

lessons.title: A frame-locked game hides cost from pace numbers: judge lateness per update
lessons.text: A game that HALTs (or waits N interrupts) per update turns a small lateness into a whole lost frame, so a window on target can cost 20 ms depending on phase (Gunrunner: a few ms at run start moved the slowest 20 updates from +2.6% to +20.9% with no slower code; Flying Shark: when the handler overruns two frames the update takes three, so a few hundred T moves whole updates). Pace can read 0.00% whatever the update costs inside (Into the Eagle's Nest), so compare cycles from the wait's end to the update's end as well, and log where the HALT lands (Ghosts n Goblins: cut only until the late tail fits; hook time fell 12% and lost frames 38 -> 8). The frame sync can hide in the sound routine (Midnight Resistance has no HALT and no FRAMES read; Cobra's beeper plays only while waiting for the interrupt, so port FE writes fell 8% in busy scenes and the limiter and prepared patterns restored 510.4 / 509.6 a second), so check frames per update before writing 'no frame sync'. Bias long windows fast and re-measure at every level after any byte change.

lessons.title: A frame that overruns one interrupt at 28 MHz costs a whole extra interrupt; measure the whole frame and credit lost interrupts
lessons.text: In Rainbow Islands the game frame runs with interrupts off and is paced at one update per 3 interrupts; a frame longer than 20 ms misses the interrupt it spans and that cycle takes 4 (a 1/50 s hitch), which on hardware happened to about a third of game frames (20-35% on island 1, 51-55% on island 7). Tracking the raster line during the frame and crediting 1 or 2 missed interrupts to the frame limiter (up to a 60 ms frame) removed most slowdowns, and the owner confirmed on a real Next that it works very well. Measure the whole game frame (original T plus hook T at 28 MHz): the old verifier under-counted long frames because rzxplay zeroes T before next_frame, so the per-frame T accumulator always added 0 and frames spanning several RZX frames lost their T; the fix needed one monotonic beam formula, an exact beam model and handling of recordings cut mid-render. Real hardware adds wait states at 28 MHz (factor 8/6.5 used in the notes), so simulated times are optimistic.

lessons.title: RZX files recorded with Fuse autosave 'off' often still hold autosave snapshots
lessons.text: Rainbow Islands (both recordings), Everyone's a Wally (12 snapshots) and Chuckie Egg (9-10) were all recorded with autosave supposedly off yet contained autosave snapshots, and an unstripped RZX desyncs on replay. Count the snapshots in every RZX and strip them (keeps the first snapshot; replay continues from the simulated state, like rzxplay --flags 4). The first RZX snapshot is SZX and a later moment than the .z80 unless 'Record from snapshot' was used; the 'ZXPR' warning is harmless. rzx info still reports the segment count after stripping.

lessons.title: Generated status/verification views conflict on every merge: rebuild, never hand-edit
lessons.text: STATUS.md, VERIFICATION.md, verified.json and the technique card index are generated from the evidence records, and parallel game PRs conflict in them and in the engines table at the end of a list. Recipe (used for nine PRs): merge main into the branch, take main's copy, keep every game's line in the engine list (hand-merge only real code conflicts such as engines.py, and keep both sides of changelogs), rerun the records views and card-index tools, run doccheck, then merge one PR at a time because the next will conflict again. Save regenerated files with LF on Windows and recheck doc size budgets (25,000-byte limit, LF, enforced by CI; learncheck requires a lesson line whenever a game note changes, so history moves to the reference repo and big notes are consolidated). Record 'next' fields feed the STATUS row, so update the record when the plan changes. When two sides carry different build hashes take the newer stamp, but it was stamped against the other side's code: if the merged change alters build bytes (for example an alt-ROM fix-up), those builds need a fresh selftest --verify --stamp.

lessons.title: gh pr merge does not wait for CI; check the checks before merging
lessons.text: In the nexclash repo, gh pr merge merged a PR whose doc check was still failing, turning main red until a follow-up PR fixed it. Editing a game notes file without adding a lesson line also fails the learning-loop rule. Check gh pr checks has passed before every merge.

lessons.title: Keys and signatures that identify a graphic or figure entry can collide, repeat, match in another order or move
lessons.text: Three 8-bit keys (sum, sum of sums, rotate and XOR) gave two of Simpsons' striped poles the same keys, while a sum plus a 16-bit hash with the size had no clash in 1,239 shapes; Crystal Kingdom Dizzy's sum-based signature matched rows in a different order, so mix the position into the signature (rotate before add / xor). A converted-pattern store keyed by stream bytes alone shares one entry between graphics with equal bytes: colours need address (+ shift) in the key (Rainbow Islands). A sprite table entry with no rows can share the address of a real one (Scooby-Doo). Keying a sprite to a figure entry's address fails when the game swaps entries to sort them (That Sinking Feeling: a figure vanished and another doubled for a frame; the flicker tool found it, the replay's sprite check did not).

lessons.title: Graphics can be mirrored, shifted or animated in place at run time: compare with the snapshot and capture from one consistent state
lessons.text: Compare in-play graphics with the snapshot before matching or painting: Solomon's Key's frame set is mirrored in place (a graphics diff between frames found 43,209 bytes), Scooby-Doo's 61.5% byte match was sprites mirrored at run time, Three Weeks frame 0 differs from its snapshot bytes and the spear carrier mirrors, Rainbow Islands' shifted-in-place player frames are stored serpentine (odd rows shifted the other way, 927 pixels), Starquake's four shifts are four animation frames, and That Sinking Feeling's jellyfish tentacles are yellow at even shifts and red at odd (count colours per shift). Walk the sprite table or census by plot before calling a set unmatched. A game that mirrors a frame in place flips graphic and mask together, so catalogue graphics written over a mirrored state got a mirrored mask in Trueno: hash the graphics at each frame end, expect transient half-mirrored states of 1-6 frames, group by mirror and keep the real ones, and take shapes from one snapshot state (Trueno builds from the state after 5000 frames).

lessons.title: Search results for graphics need confirming by pointers or replay
lessons.text: A graphic search over the whole snapshot found 1,028 matches in Phantis; only those the code points at, or a replay really plots, are graphics (166). A plot whose save-under pointer is in ROM is a permanent stamp (scenery), not a figure (Nemesis): check every plot caller's save pointer before treating it as a sprite.

lessons.title: A game that draws only grid-aligned blocks needs no plot hooks
lessons.text: Gauntlet: the picture is looked up from the finished hidden screen, so nothing of the game is touched and scrolling needs no tracking. Pictures no recording shows can come from the game's own tables, but anything drawn at pixel positions (shots) has no finite set of cells: decide that at design stage, not after the painting.

lessons.title: Unit-test every guard edge: out-of-range plots must pass through exactly as the guard says
lessons.text: Guards that turn overflow cases (buffer or attribute overflow, table full, no sprites left, hen outside table) into unchanged ULA passthrough need unit tests at each edge, checking converted versus passthrough matches the guard exactly. A code path no RZX reaches can be proven by a unit differential test from the same state plus a negative control that must fail.

lessons.title: Cross-check hand-assembled hooks with sjasmplus; known assembler quirks
lessons.text: A hand-assembled hook had a JR out of range that went unnoticed: assert sjasmplus output equals the Python emitter and use JP for long branches; a reassembled hook file must equal the profile hex. sjasmplus quirks: use --zxnext; 'pair' is a reserved word (label error); po (parity odd, as in call po) is a Z80 condition code and sjasmplus refused it as a routine name (Nemesis, renamed pout), so avoid names that are condition codes or mnemonics; ld a,(EXPR) assembles as a memory read even when EXPR is a constant (Atic Atac), so use an EQU; local labels inside a MACRO are macro-local, so inline the text when the macro jumps to the enclosing routine's label. On Windows, pass forward slashes to sjasmplus.

lessons.title: The model must expose only the actual hidden-ROM span when its page is unmapped
lessons.text: Bruce Lee: exposing the whole private page 24 hid two native entry/exit failures; expose just the real span.

lessons.title: Owner rule: remove tape-loading prompts and start at the first real screen
lessons.text: The project owner asked that converted .nex builds drop the tape loading status messages and key waits (REWIND SIDE 2, LOADING..., LOADED OK, STOP TAPE) so the first screen shown is the game's own first real screen; for R-Type that is the specification screen with the ship designs, held 5 seconds or until a key or fire, then the logo and title. The game still unpacks each level, just without the prompts.

lessons.title: hlib_pace_open / hlib_debt_open lose registers; library changes can move verified bytes
lessons.text: The current hlib_pace_open and hlib_debt_open lose DE (V1 kept it) (Cobra) and hlib_debt_open loses HL (Comando Quatro): save or take the game's value from its saved copy. Beyond the Ice Palace: main's pace library moved the engine's bytes; DEFINE HLIB_PACE_V1 keeps the verified build (as Cobra, Gryzor and Cauldron 1.1).

lessons.title: Many small calls: getting to 28 MHz costs more than it saves
lessons.text: Running the cell hooks at 28 MHz cut 124 frames to 94, not to the original's 58, because a hook called 5,500 times spends most of its time getting there (a PC sample by NR 7 showed it at once). Simpsons: a wait per figure cost about 1,600 T of 3.5 MHz time each, more than the saving on small figures; one window round the whole draw pass fixed it. Mixing speeds by call count is chaotic when the speed also carries past the loop: tune with something uniform per call.

lessons.title: A private hook stack removes dead-stack residue from whole-RAM compare
lessons.text: A private stack inside the mapped hook page removes dead game-stack residue so full 48K native comparison needs no stack exclusions (Gunfright). A hook that CALLs on the game's own stack changes dead bytes visible in lockstep (Ikari Warriors), so hide hooks were made stackless.

lessons.title: A hook must leave every register as the original would at the resume address; a register that looks dead can be live and SP may be a data pointer
lessons.text: The verifier compares at the resume PC, so even registers the game overwrites next must match (Rainbow 60965: HL; 60839: the carry that the replaced DEC A leaves); loop control can live in AF' (Rainbow plotters), so restore AF' and all registers before re-running game code, and inside a hook that calls a helper reload every register the helper clobbered (Chuckie's e_hd used C after the helper had changed BC; found by reading before the first run). Simpsons: the game's SP is its data pointer inside the draw routine, so a hook there has no stack until it sets its own, and a register that looks dead (C at the shape) is live on the early exits. Rambo: the blit's BC is B from its own LD and C=0 left by the wait, so the first commit lost C and ran off the table (lockstep found it at once). Olli and Lissa 2: a hook saving AF on the game's stack before switching writes two bytes below the game's SP, found by comparing all game memory; HLIB_R_IN goes after the stack switch.

lessons.title: Identical measurements after a change mean the harness reused old code or a stale build
lessons.text: In Inferno the verifier's store cache key did not cover the pattern-selection code, so a re-measurement silently reused the old code; it was caught only because the numbers came out identical to the previous run. A pace script that built its fixture only when the file was missing measured a build from hours earlier under a reused tag (Gunrunner): use a new tag per measurement and build once before the runs start. When a change that should move a measurement leaves it exactly unchanged, check the harness cache key and the build's freshness before trusting the result.

lessons.title: Routines reachable from both ISR and ordinary code, and nested drawing, need their IFF saved and audited
lessons.text: A sound call inside an ISR can also be reached by ordinary code: preserve its incoming IFF, protect shared hook state before the first write and compare both IFF states (Treasure Island Dizzy); SkoolKit's per-call int_active of 32 can clear both LD A,I PV reads without an accepted interrupt, paired-hook simulators use 0 and real injected IRQs are tested separately (Underwurlde), and fixed-M1 IFF reads need equal fetch counts on both paths. Inner drawing overwrites its IFF latch, so an outer wrapper needs its own saved IFF (Movie); a single LD A,I read was trusted after one read in Incredible Shrinking Fireman, the shared hooklib.iff_audit now fails any such read in asm/ (demonstrated by selftest --tools), and a full replay exposed 19 IFF-enabled sprite updates.

lessons.title: Trace the IM 2 route through FFFF; the slot-0 page owns the interrupt
lessons.text: The IM2 JR at FFFF reads its offset from 0000, so the slot-0 page owns the IRQ and the original's no-op ISR (T, M1) must be counted rather than lost under DI (Inferno). Head Over Heels' real route is FFFF to FFF4 to 7376, and the reference should start at interrupt acknowledgement, not assume an R count at ISR entry. Interrupt injection should traverse the whole route through RET including unwind.

lessons.title: When importing an external colour conversion, import by graphics address, never its snapshot
lessons.text: Dizzy Ultimate: the colour conversion's graphics matched all 78 player frames and 256 plotter-2 images, but its snapshot differed in state, title data and the lives instruction; import colours by graphics address and never copy its executable snapshot.

lessons.title: Importing an engine onto a newer main
lessons.text: Rebuild on main first and compare bytes: a shared stub piece had moved (436 bytes, New Zealand Story); a branch from an older main is upstreamed by checking main's copy equals the branch's base, then judging each main-only fix (Quazatron); frozen files plus reviewed registry patches rebuilt both NEX byte for byte, so the proof carried (Underwurlde, shown by rebuilding and comparing); an approved build made before new defaults rebuilds only with its pin (Three Weeks); a pilot's change to a shared boot model goes into the engine on import (Spellbound).

lessons.title: Incremental-draw engines need one sprite per object, set at plot and hidden at erase and clear
lessons.text: A game with no full redraw (erase = tile redraw at the old position, draw = OR or overwrite at the new one) needs no staging or commit: set the object's sprite at its plot, hide it at its erase and at every screen clear. Chuckie Egg used sprites 0-4 hens, 5 duck, 6 player. Known visual differences stay (a figure the original skipped drawing is visible, no ghost where the original skipped an erase).

lessons.title: Report display publication separately from pace; each added layer raised the drop rate
lessons.text: For the Inferno sprite window work, publication rate, longest miss run and maximum displayed-state age are measured separately from pace, and assumed spare time is not a budget. Simulator figures climbed as layers were added: dropped updates 12.3% (scenery) to 14.9% (dispatch) to 18.5% (pattern store), longest run 6 to 14 to 32 updates, about 0.8 s stale. The 8EF9 pause modelled at 4.9 s was about 4 s on a real Next with speed and beeper unchanged. Re-measure the cumulative figure after each layer.

lessons.title: Per-update pattern uploads are tiny after the initial set; do the initial set in a load pause
lessons.text: A simulator census of the first 5,000 frames per Inferno level (64 slots, current and pending protected) gave a median of 0 uploads per update and a 99th percentile of at most 6, with the maximum being the first update (up to 47). So the initial pattern set should be uploaded in the pause before the level. On level 1, 8 of 1,053 updates needed more than 64 protected patterns. Uploading 56 patterns by CPU each update would cost 16.7 ms, too long for a window as short as 4.4 ms.

lessons.title: One palette offset can hold all Spectrum inks if the ink is part of the pattern
lessons.text: A dedicated 4-bit palette offset with index 1 black, 2-8 normal ink and 9-15 bright ink (Next default ULA levels) lets one offset serve every ink; Rainbow offset 15 coloured items in their cell ink. In MAME, a palette-offset silhouette made index 0 opaque (whole 16x16 boxes), so check transparency per emulator.

lessons.title: Fix colour clash on a figure the game colours by OR-ing ink into a rectangle of cells by drawing it as hardware sprites
lessons.text: In Cisco Heat the player's car turned road lines, posts and other cars red because the game colours it by writing ink over a rectangle of attribute cells. Drawing the car as red hardware sprites of the game's own pixels, covering only the cells the original turned red, over the game's black pixels removed the clash and left the shadow black. Sprites matched the original's red pixels exactly in all 103 test frames including mirrored images, using the ULA palette copied into the sprite palette, the sprite mirror flag and the clip window. Hardware reported it works.

lessons.title: Interrupt checks need timing evidence, not only counts and injection
lessons.text: Injection checks alone missed a native stack race; count original handler entries as well as hardware acknowledgements, and re-run the known failing input. Equal counts do not prove equal timing (a 25.132 ms gap needed a per-row poll).
