Added drawing can place a ULA pulse inside an original sound-bank DI window: trace the interrupted PC and recover the pending pulse between drawing spans rather than changing the sound routine. Polling every row adds cost if the row never disables interrupts (poll every few rows).

lessons.title: A handler that re-enables interrupts within ~40 T runs twice per frame on the Next core
lessons.text: A handler that enables interrupts within about 40 T of the acknowledge is re-entered on the Next core; a 128K's 36 T /INT pulse hides it, and emulators that take one interrupt per frame never show it. Altered Beast's crash was found on the board, not in any simulator: interrupt length is a hardware-only fact.

lessons.title: Interrupts taken per second is a pace too; DI stretches lose interrupts
lessons.text: A stack wipe under DI lost 6% of the interrupts, so game clock and music would have run slow with update pace in range (Silkworm; interrupts on between rows fixed it). A hook pair that held DI for every hook lost two interrupts in a row at room builds (Spellbound, 49.45 a second; only the slot-5 remap needed DI). A turbo limiter running the game frame with interrupts off loses the interrupts a long frame spans (Rainbow Islands engine). Read 'interrupts taken' beside update pace.

lessons.title: Black attributes and INK=PAPER hide bitmap bytes; colour layers must reproduce the visibility
lessons.text: Original INK=PAPER can hide an intact bitmap, so an opaque colour layer must reproduce that visibility change; matching bitmap bytes alone does not prove the ending screen (Highway Encounter). Black attributes hide stale bitmap bytes: compare visible colours while retaining original bytes (Inferno).

lessons.title: Do not wrap the game's interrupt handler; use a second vector selected by I inside hooks
lessons.text: A handler a few T short of or past a whole number of frames decides whether the game gets a frame between notes: Booty's 300 T wrapper on every interrupt took a death's room from 36 frames to 94. Use a second vector selected by I only while inside hooks (Bruce Lee's private IM2 vector lets the original ISR run during hook work without rewriting the original vector; save its actual interrupted clock and use a separate IRQ stack).

lessons.title: JNext's 28 MHz is not 8x: the ratio varies by game, scene and routine, so measure it per game and live
lessons.text: Quazatron routines ran only 5 to 6.5 times faster at 28 MHz than at 3.5 MHz (wait states vs contention), moving by routine (5.0 to 6.6); a K borrowed from another game read 25% long on Renegade (6.6 there). In Hard Drivin' JNext's ratio ranged 6.17 to 6.28 by scene and Castle Master was calibrated at 6.75 on JNext only (repo notes give 6.6-7.0 for hardware; hardware values still unmeasured). Rainbow Islands engine: simulated 28 MHz T times 8/6.5 turned 13 simulated overruns into 128 hardware ones in 1,043 frames (inferred from board figures). Measure K per game, and per routine when a fast window is used; averaging measurements lagged the scene (after 178 updates the build ran 18 frames ahead), while using the latest measurement and re-measuring every 16 updates cut that to 4 (a measuring update has no time for extra views, about 4% fewer).

lessons.title: Program DMA port cycle length: reset timing is far slower
lessons.text: In JNext 1.1.104, DMA with both ports at cycle length 2 took 3.6 T a byte against 12.5 with the reset timing (Scooby-Doo): program the timing. Zero-filling empty pattern quadrants with ordinary DMA avoided per-cell blank writes (R-Type: live 23-sprite preparation 47.687 ms, down from 66.915 ms).

lessons.title: An execute probe or breakpoint can fire twice when an interrupt lands on it
lessons.text: A probe, rule or breakpoint at an address that runs with interrupts on fires twice when an interrupt lands on it, before the instruction actually runs: Head Over Heels (count effects at the instruction after the original DI with the argument loaded, and do not read an entry duplicate as a second effect), New Zealand Story (a false update parted lockstep; guarded in the pace profile), R-Type (JNext reports an execute address again after an IRQ; use one-shot phase flags and nested-ledger negatives), Booty (a probe at a loop head gave one extra update and read as a run shifted by one; the pace script now ignores a second firing within 20,000 T) and Dizzy Ultimate (the event can occur both before and after an accepted interrupt at the same CALL, so rearm at the actual return and count completed updates, never both notifications).

lessons.title: Isolate JNext with its own config and temp folders for parallel agents
lessons.text: JNEXT_CONFIG_DIR isolates JNext without changing HOME (Dizzy Ultimate); Bruce Lee used private JNext config/temp folders. Master cards stay read-only and actual-loader tests use disposable copies. Abu Simbel noted JNext was slow when other agents' runs were active.

lessons.title: JNext 1.3.0 does not emulate the zxnDDMA blitter; CSpect 4.5.9 does
lessons.text: A self-checking probe ran classic copy, 2D fill, 2D strided copy, 2D transparent copy and physical-address 2D fill: CSpect passed all, JNext passed only the classic copy; on the board the results matched CSpect and timings were within 1-3 video lines. Use CSpect for blitter work and the board for timing; JNext only covers CPU fallback paths, and any path using the blitter (including the blitter-first shared DMA library) can time slower there than on hardware, so treat those figures as worst case. Physical addressing: 8K page n sits at $040000 + n*$2000 (Inferno: plain zxnDMA continuous copy was used for one contiguous 1,152-byte block since the blitter's 2D modes add nothing there and DMA is about 4x faster than the CPU). JNext headless runs on a private copy of the SD image and never writes it back, so persistence of SD saves across power cycles cannot be tested in JNext.

lessons.title: JNext facts: only it shows a Next's palette and true screen; execute-triggered saves land at frame end
lessons.text: The simulator and emuspec256 show the plain palette; only JNext shows what a Next shows (Page Pharaoh). Phantis: a verifier checked its own idea of the column and only the JNext screen showed the overlay one column left. In JNext 1.2.0 execute-triggered JNS save requests land at a frame boundary, so exact hook ABI/RAM tests use execute-time logs or dump_mem instead (R-Type). Frame-edge snapshots can catch a correct hook halfway through an upload: diagnose persistence and inspect rendered frames before calling it corruption (Nodes of Yesod).

lessons.title: JNext rewrites A at ROM PC 056B while its tape trap is on
lessons.text: New code placed in old tape ROM must avoid PC 056B because JNext rewrites A there while its tape trap is on (Inferno: hooks at 04C6/0574).

lessons.title: Keep the .nex's game memory identical to the snapshot except the patch sites
lessons.text: Design rule for mods that must be distributable as a difference: patch sites small (a 3-byte jump or single data bytes, each listing original bytes and refusing a snapshot that differs); put hook code and data in the alt ROM and free Next RAM banks, never relocate or repack game code; a start-up tail only in memory proven unused. Trueno's .nex had 63,661 bytes copied from the snapshot against 157,537 own bytes (hooks, patterns, Layer 2 tables).

lessons.title: Layer 2 640x256 scrolls in whole Spectrum pixels; half-pixel steps need two screens
lessons.text: Layer 2 at 640x256 scrolls in whole Spectrum pixels. R-Type reached half-pixel steps by keeping two screens, one shifted half a pixel, and showing them alternately from the interrupt. The tilemap's 80-column offset is in half pixels but could not hold R-Type's tiles: the tilemap's map and tiles must live in bank 5 or in the lower 8 KB of bank 7 on newer cores, and R-Type's live data fills bank 5 while bank 7 held packed levels.

lessons.title: Colour a 1-bit view on Layer 2 by keeping the game's buffer pixels
lessons.text: Building the Layer 2 picture from the game's own 1-bit buffer (set pixel takes the face colour, clear pixel the area's paper) keeps the dither exactly and brings back anything the game draws into that buffer (message scrolls, centre marker) for free. Colouring a whole byte by pattern matching gave black blocks at face edges; flat per-face fills hid text. What the game draws straight onto the ULA screen (cursor) or only into attributes (interrupt colour cycle) is lost under the layer and needs a sprite and a palette change. A see-through-ULA alternative has an unsolved problem when the panel shares the view's paper colour.

lessons.title: Replaying drawing commands at the producers' entries beat shadow renderers
lessons.text: Four colour shadows of the original renderer stayed slower than the original (Gunfright: +2.4% quiet, +52% duel). Recording commands at the producers' entries, after the original computed address, data, rows, shift and mirror, and replaying them in order into a hidden Layer 2 buffer brought every scene within 2%: the original drawing keeps running, so RAM and R parity are free and only the replay costs time.

lessons.title: A copy at the right edge carries into the next row or D: LDI at column 255 of Layer 2, a tile at column 31
lessons.text: LDI's DE carries out of column 255 into the next row, so a tile at the right edge of Layer 2 needs its last byte by hand; the whole-picture replay model caught it where hook registers and RAM alone did not (Page Pharaoh). A verifier check written for another game's plotter (a figure wraps within its row) failed a third of Pssst's edge cases because that plotter runs on into the next row. Copying a tile at column 31 carried into D, so push and pop DE per row rather than trusting E to wrap (Eagle's Nest).

lessons.title: Drawing moving figures into a scrolling Layer 2 is costly
lessons.text: For R-Type, drawing overflow figures into Layer 2 would mean erasing and restoring the scenery under them on both half-pixel screens every update, the figures would step in whole 8-pixel cells without glide, and a hull drawn there would cover figures if Layer 2 sits above sprites. A zxnDDMA estimate gave about 77 KB per move for the hull, roughly one frame. Layer 2 only fits something that behaves like scenery.

lessons.title: LD A,I reads P/V as 0 if an interrupt is accepted during it; SkoolKit applies this on its own frame timing, so IFF reads must be doubled
lessons.text: On NMOS Z80s the interrupt-flag read via LD A,I can be wrong; read it twice (ld a,i / jp pe,ok / ld a,i), and hooklib.iff_audit demands two reads (3D Stock Car, Chase H.Q.: a single read is not safe). SkoolKit's Simulator models the quirk from its own 48K frame timing, not the harness's interrupts, so in a harness that injects its own interrupts a safe interrupts-off/on macro left interrupts off at random and hung a test run (Castle Master HLIB_IFF_DI): set int_active 0 and clear P/V only where the harness actually accepts an interrupt. Bruce Lee: a direct-opcode scope must set int_active=0 when it delivers no interrupts, and real delivery is tested separately with the instruction-boundary injection matrix.

lessons.title: LDI's flag bits 3 and 5 depend on the byte copied
lessons.text: A blit whose source changes differs in F bits 3 and 5 after LDI; check the bits are dead rather than masking all of F (Ikari Warriors). Also, the simulator's LDIX family once dropped writes below 0x4000 so the verifier's write map showed nothing though JNext was right; sim.low_writes lets a model see them (Mad Mix 2).

lessons.title: Legacy 7FFD/1FFD writes remap MMU slots; ordering and lock behaviour
lessons.text: An unlocked legacy write remaps MMU slots 0/1 (ROM) and 6/7, and the most recent change wins, so map a RAM slot-1 page AFTER the tail's own paging writes. 128K: an unlocked write remaps C000-FFFF at once. Reading of the VHDL (3.01.09, not confirmed on hardware): locked writes (7FFD bit 5 = 1) are ignored without remapping, NextReg $08 bit 7 can only unlock, and 48K timing (NextReg $03) does NOT stop 7FFD/1FFD decoding; an earlier note that it changes port decoding was wrong but harmless. Pages mapped into slot 0 with interrupts on risk a crash (IM1 vector at 0x38), and code in slot 0 cannot unmap slot 0.

lessons.title: Reading the line clock needs a lock-free retry, and readings a frame apart jitter
lessons.text: Cisco Heat: `now` under DI took longer than the INT pulse at 28 MHz so every interrupt in a hook wait was lost; read lock-free and again if the clock moved. The interrupt lands on the same video line, so lines since the last read are 0 mod 311 at each interrupt (add a frame when under half of one). Castle Master: two line readings a frame apart differ by 0 or 311.

lessons.title: The loader clears NR 0x08 bit 1 after set-up
lessons.text: 3D Stock Car: the loader clears NR 0x08 bit 1 (second sound chip, turbosound) after the setup stub; a hook that needs the second chip must set it itself.

lessons.title: Counting hook instructions out keeps original and patched machines in lockstep
lessons.text: If hook instructions are counted as nothing, the original and patched machines stay in lockstep with the whole 128K compared per frame and no per-site pairing; this works only where game instructions stay the same (Knight Tyme).

lessons.title: Lockstep RZX replay cannot prove a patched game equivalent; test per routine from real states
lessons.text: Once hooks change cycle counts, input sampling shifts and the replay diverges, so lockstep comparison proves nothing. The method that worked on every game: replay the original, and at each patched routine copy the state, run original and patched code to the return and compare all registers (except R, T, MEMPTR) and all memory. Registers that differ at the return are acceptable only if stepping both copies shows they converge or are overwritten before use.

lessons.title: Long verifies and background jobs: use the harness's background mode, no time limit, and kill by PID
lessons.text: setsid nohup jobs died with the tool call while the harness's own background mode worked (Lode Runner); $! after setsid nohup is the wrapper's PID so a kill -0 wait ended at once (Jetpac); a /dev/null stdin overrides a Python heredoc (Inferno). A background command given a time limit is stopped at the limit, so run long checks with none (Olli and Lissa 2); five full runs in parallel take about 25 minutes and auto prints nothing until it ends (Simpsons); a cheat test passed the shell time limit at load 60 (Eagle's Nest); a full Lunar Jetman verify takes about 80 min detached; a survey of an 83,418-frame recording did not finish in 15 minutes and was rerun with --stop 15000, and a 64-minute survey of a 63-minute recording needed a warning and reuse (Trap Door); a heavily loaded machine left a long shell command unstarted (Ruff and Reddy: use separate short ones). Killing a selftest leaves worker processes, so kill the auto child's PID too and never pkill -f (Robin of the Wood; Knight Tyme); a wait loop written as kill -0 $(pgrep -o -f X) is the same warned pattern in a new form (Nemesis). Inferno's doccheck counts CRLF bytes unless core.autocrlf is false.

lessons.title: A frame interrupt that comes and goes while a hook has interrupts off can be detected with NextReg $C8 and compensated
lessons.text: When a hook or window runs with interrupts off, a frame interrupt pulse can start and end unseen. Inferno's copier window and hooks read NextReg $C8 to see that the pulse happened and then add what the original interrupt handler would have done (its T-states, and its effect on R, applying the no-op ISR), which removed the 0.09% of lost IRQs seen in milestone 2. A small gap remained in the model: a pulse starting in the few T between the last $C8 check and re-enabling interrupts is still lost.

lessons.title: Machine.run(addr) returns at once when already at the stop address
lessons.text: Cisco Heat: run(0x8BE1) returns immediately if the machine is already there, so step one instruction between updates.

lessons.title: Run the game's main loop at 28 MHz and keep the interrupt handler at 3.5 MHz when sound runs in the ISR
lessons.text: In R-Type both beeper routines run only from the interrupt handler, so the game logic, plotters and copier can run at 28 MHz while the ISR wrapper drops to 3.5 MHz for the original ISR code and keeps sound pitch and timing. On the same 100-update busy stretch the original took 10.516 s, the 3.5 MHz sprite build 11.665 s (10.9% slower) and the 28 MHz build 9.679 s (7.96% faster); interrupts stayed at 50 Hz. Check first which routines the ISR calls and which code really needs exact timing; the owner accepted dropping the original's busy-scene slowdown here.

lessons.title: make_nfo always writes the clash-fix paragraph
lessons.text: The nxc repo's tools/make_nfo.py always writes the clash-fix paragraph, so a game with no clash (Atom Ant) needs it reworded by hand.

lessons.title: Preserve the original mask and ink composition; masks are not binary transparency
lessons.text: Some source ink bits lie outside the mask (Gunfright), so mask-only extraction loses pixels: keep mask OR ink as support. Head Over Heels colour masks are not binary transparency (ignoring painted bits made a hollow image) so keep the original AND/OR per plane. Knight Lore likewise needs the original opaque masks and plot order, coincident ink included, because a final monochrome buffer does not establish coloured pixel ownership.

lessons.title: Measure where a redraw spends its time before reaching for DMA or the blitter
lessons.text: R-Type's 640-cell level-start draw took 42 frames; disabling the sky cells in memory (a quick breakpoint-frame test) showed sky cells cost about 25 frames and scenery cells about 17. A scenery cell cost about 100,000 cycles to compute (mask and colour lookup) but wrote only 64 bytes, so a blitter would save a few hundred cycles per cell and zxnDDMA had no measurable payoff. Skipping sky cells whose left neighbour is not scenery (needed for the half-pixel carry on screen B) cut the draw to 17 frames with both Layer 2 screens byte-identical.

lessons.title: Verifier cases that start mid-routine or at a waiting routine
lessons.text: A set-up that other routines enter past its start cannot tell the hook whose figure it is from IX alone: the game's own entry marks the draw and an unmarked one changes nothing; an event that starts mid-draw must be given what earlier hooks left (the mark), or it tests a state the game never has (all 794 Tranz Am draws failed until it was). A CALL before a routine that waits for keys (the title) cannot be compared at the routine's end from a copy of the state: compare where it starts (Olli and Lissa 2).

lessons.title: Choose the MMU slot for hook pages by what the game, ISR, stack and hook itself use; read game bytes before remapping
lessons.text: Choose the slot by what the game and ISR touch: Silkworm's ISR runs through slot 7 (read the isr Slots line; slot 5 was free); Solomon's Key has its stack at the top of memory so the state page maps at slot 6; at NEX start-up SP is near DFEE in slot 6, so mapping any page there crashed R-Type (use slots 3 and 7 for the start-up code's own mappings and restore them; routines called from start-up code must save HL themselves if the shared g_call does not). A 7FFD write maps ROM over slots 0-1: an ISR (That Sinking Feeling) or the level unpack (R-Type) hides a hook page or stack in slot 1, so return through game RAM that maps the hook page back before EI; a hook at a site with interrupts on must not map the state page over the ROM's handler before DI (Olli and Lissa), while a pattern page at a slot the handler never reads needs no DI (Renegade; at slot 0 an interrupt went astray). A hook that clears a busy flag by mapping a page into the MMU slot it executes from loses its code and hangs (Inferno, slot 1; the simulator test missed it because its harness ignored the mapping): map into another slot and make the harness model MMU mappings. In a hook that remaps a slot, read the game's bytes first: Atic Atac (IX object before remapping slot 6/7), Booty (reading tables after mapping slot 5 over them gave a width of 0), Abu Simbel (reads in the remapped slot can still decide the path, BIT 6 on attributes, so R and time differed until the attributes were copied into the scratch page); Green Beret: redirecting slot 2 keeps every register and the timing with almost no hook code if the game does not read the screen for logic and the ISR stays out of slot 2.

lessons.title: Model the NEX launch state from hardware evidence, not the worst case
lessons.text: A boot model that assumed 7FFD locked at launch rejected every hardware-proven build; at NEX launch paging is unlocked. The boot check's expected ROM view must include the register block the stub writes (it first showed 17 'ROM differs' bytes there), and a deliberately broken stub (no 1FFD write, no unlock, hooks not copied) must fail it.

lessons.title: When game code reads R, place the original run's interrupt at the same game instruction as the patched run
lessons.text: Inferno level 2 diverged between the original and patched models until the original's interrupt was placed at the same game instruction where the patched run took or compensated it, as an RZX recording does. Level 6 also reads R, and every original copier head contains at least one frame IRQ, so the window adds the original's interrupt routine cost (94 T, 10 to R) when it takes one. Matching by time instead of instruction gives false differences for any game that reads R.

lessons.title: A model that starts from a snapshot cannot see boot-time damage: boot the real NEX, and keep hooks off the stub's register block in the alt ROM
lessons.text: Inferno's capture-hook crash passed every simulator check because the model starts from game state and never runs the NEX loader or startup stub; a window-only diagnostic worked on hardware while the hook build crashed, which pointed at the boot path. The NEX startup stub restores the game's registers from a 20-byte block it writes into the alt ROM (about 0x3945-0x3958) at boot; the first build put helper routines at 0x3948, so the first hook jumped into register bytes and on hardware crashed every time with many vertical green bars while the build without hooks ran. Fix: move the hooks to 0x3960 and add a build check that boots each actual .nex in the simulator and requires every hook byte to be intact afterwards; do not treat a model pass as proof the NEX starts.

lessons.title: A monochrome game or play area needs no hook site; the build is the conversion
lessons.text: For a monochrome game with no figures to hook, no site is needed; the checks that still mean something are the boot compare with R, rom_paths over the system ROM, the tail reads and lockstep runs against the original (Gunrunner, Jilly's Farm, Atom Ant). R has no hook to be compared at, and the notes say so.

lessons.title: A multi-load tape game can be built as one NEX by hooking the menu's tape-load routine
lessons.text: Winter Sports loads six 32 KB events over the menu from tape, each with a 22-byte pseudo-header, which the standard TAP's 19-byte headers do not match; nexclash finds tape blocks by content, so the TAP is still valid input. The plain NEX embeds all events in banks and a 127-byte hook in unused menu memory copies the chosen event instead of reading tape. Hardware confirmed it loads and Downhill runs. The Bleepload re-release's loading screen is inside the turbo loader, so it cannot be an accepted tape set.

lessons.title: Native screenshot and timing captures need completed frames
lessons.text: A screenshot requested at an instruction-boundary freeze may hold the preceding partial video frame (Gunfright: wait two complete frozen frames to remove an isolated HUD mismatch). Exiting immediately after requesting a screenshot returned an error despite valid timing data (Martianoids): allow the final frame to complete and compare only completed update intervals.

lessons.title: Timing claims and limiter constants come from native measurements, not simulator T counts
lessons.text: Producer hooks inside a measured render window lengthen it and are scaled by the limiter's slope; refit the constants from native measurements (Gunfright). Native whole-publication measurements, not simulator T counts, establish a DMA fallback's benefit. Estimates must be labelled separately from native pace (Head Over Heels). Raster samples omit wrapper entry/exit and gaps between window samples, so profile those native offsets before fixing a debt (Highway Encounter).

lessons.title: Start native trials from the game's own boundary, not a convenient checkpoint
lessons.text: Bruce Lee: resume before E200 and preserve the original prefix; a title checkpoint hides loader state and is not an archive-to-build boot proof. Bubbler: fixed video-frame snapshots can land in the game's pause loop, so capture the original player-update boundary. Exolon: mid-game fixtures must seed active XOR effects or the first erase is mistaken for a new draw.

lessons.title: A negative control must be shown to fail and must change a path the recording actually reaches
lessons.text: A negative passes or goes n/a silently unless the data reaches the broken path: read the detected counts, count n/a explicitly, run every new negative once and aim each at what the recording runs (a MISSED one is a finding about the negative or the recording). Examples: Wally's unit test reloaded the whole captured RAM page and put the good table back over the broken one; Rainbow's two figure controls read live sprite attributes after the commit moved them and reported n/a on all 40 states for 9 days (check against the state the hook produces, staged not live); Chuckie's duck blank frame draws no pixels; corrupting one LUT entry escaped four recorded frames (Gunfright: corrupt every entry; Dynamite Dan: mutate all table entries); Lunar Jetman's evict negative passed a 700-frame replay because the pool never filled; a negative line printed inside a PASSED stamp did not count (Jet Set Willy); Movie's transparency negatives need a nonempty overlap and the broken patch's own code and tables; Knight Tyme's composed-box blit passed every model until a ULA-equals-clean-copy check; Abu Simbel depth controls missed on room 1 but caught on attract; Finders Keepers room set-up and erase-all; Crystal Kingdom Dizzy hide hooks caught on one walk of four; Cisco Heat's negative W had no spec frames; Army Moves' capture negative passed at 900 frames before any capture; Gauntlet's 'attribute not compared' cannot fail because the attribute picks the chain; Page Pharaoh's 'XOR made plain' mutated a loop that never undraws; Phantis' clipped-row negative was never reached in 24,000 frames (and a pattern finding the first of two code copies changed the rarer one); Pac-Mania's yellow cells are invisible in a yellow room and a frame-80 sprite is blank; Spellbound's 'characters paint' undetected where character and room colour are equal; Tranz Am's control changing the first LD A,n changed the mark's constant, not R's; Robin of the Wood's leftover sys.argv MODE line made negatives run as normal. Fix with unit cases from captured states, longer stops or mutating every entry. Arc of Yesod: ten scripted recordings never showed a wrong-colour path that a human recording found within three minutes, because the searches rewarded rooms and code, not keys beyond movement.

lessons.title: Hook spans nest their inner sites; ROM routines are hooked by JPs in the build's own image
lessons.text: A hook that runs the routine to the caller's return nests the sites inside it, so the replay skips them until the span ends (Cauldron: PO-ATTR in the plot body). When no exit JP fits, the entry hook can CALL the body (show at entry, hide after). ROM routines below 0x2000 (PR-ALL, CL-LINE, CL-SCROLL, PO-ATTR) are hooked by JPs in the build's own image; scan the ROM for jumps into the replaced bytes first (PO-SCR CALLs 0x0E00 inside CL-SCROLL).

lessons.title: Never hook a timing-critical ISR such as beeper music
lessons.text: Hooking the title-screen ISR of Treasure Island Dizzy (beeper music, 63328) broke the music. Check that an ISR-called routine can take extra T before hooking it. A hook inside an ISR must also keep EXX / EX AF,AF' parity even, because the handler restores registers by set.

lessons.title: A new-code count misses a move into a place that runs the same code
lessons.text: Arc of Yesod's descent search reported nothing because the caverns reuse the surface's routines; watch a game variable (here the room number) instead of counting newly executed code.

lessons.title: A build that adds banks above 47 must say so in .nex header byte 8
lessons.text: The converter leaves byte 8 at 0; 3D Stock Car's engine sets it in auto() for a build that adds banks above 47.

lessons.title: NEX header loading screen is unreliable; owner rules for the loading screen (at least 4 s, or at ENTER in the NXC loader)
lessons.text: A NEX with a header loading screen made CSpect close and JNext skip it, and on a real Next the loader was expected to overwrite it with the first bank; holding the screen in the first loaded bank and restoring the game's screen in start-up code worked (Beyond the Ice Palace, Castle Master). Owner rules differ by target: the loading screen is displayed for at least 4 seconds immediately on launching the NEX (more if the game needs; Winter Sports holds 5.2 s in standalone NEX builds, and the files inside an NXC patch are built without the hold), while inside the NXC patch the loader shows the screen the moment ENTER is pressed via the build_screen key (offset of the screen within the tape), with dots while patching and no fixed hold. The NXC loader now reads the screen block straight from the tape (a plain 6,912-byte block) before any checking and adds a dot per bank built, confirmed on hardware; it needs a tape with an ordinary screen block, and a black blink before the game starts remains.

lessons.title: A ULA loading screen in a sjasmplus .nex must be marked as having no palette or CSpect loads everything 512 bytes out
lessons.text: sjasmplus does not mark a ULA loading screen as having no palette, so CSpect looked for one, loaded every part of the R-Type program 512 bytes out of place and crashed. The join script now sets the no-palette bit in the NEX header. Check any file that adds a loading screen; this was the first R-Type file with one and was seen in CSpect only.

lessons.title: A NEX that forces 50 Hz blanks the screen if the Next is set to 60 Hz
lessons.text: Seeing menu, black, menu at start was the video-mode switch from 60 to 50 Hz done by the start-up code (game speed is tied to 50 Hz); setting the Next to 50 Hz removed it on hardware. Running at 60 Hz does not make the game faster, since the NEX forces 50 Hz anyway. The 48K timing write (NextReg 0x03) was suspected next; a test copy without it was built but not needed.

lessons.title: nextboot ROM path check: entry boundaries need exact boot proof, and a tail jumping to boot code is credited
lessons.text: Beyond the Ice Palace: a tail that jumps to the build's own boot code, which restores 0x5B00-0x5BFF, was reported as read before written; the check now boots on to the game's PC and credits bytes back. Bubbler: a replaced BASIC loader prefix is not a runtime ROM path; an explicit entry boundary needs separate exact boot proof, records its first frame, rejects a missing entry and still catches later ROM faults.

lessons.title: NextReg $7F is a safe flag store for hooks
lessons.text: Write it with NEXTREG and read it through ports 243B (select) and 253B (data). Trueno used bit 6 of it to signal a screen shake to the commit; hooks that need no RAM page can keep a flag there.

lessons.title: The NextREG select port (0x243B) is shared state: an interrupt between OUT 243B and IN 253B breaks the read
lessons.text: An interrupt between a hook's OUT 0x243B and its IN 0x253B leaves another register selected, so the main line reads the handler's register: the speed latch took a line number or NR 0x53's page as the clock (Eagle's Nest HLIB_SPEED_IN latched a line number, found via Silkworm's pace tables; New Zealand Story ran at 28 MHz until reset; Silkworm a lone 175 ms update once in about 1,500), and Castle Master's read-back of the MMU paging registers raced the pace clock in the interrupt and would later map the wrong page, also on real hardware. Do those reads with interrupts off (Head Over Heels' mutation selector is latched inside the entry DI window, and boundary injection caught the old version when register/R and RAM still matched), or hold the latch in every interrupt and reselect NR 7 before returning, and have the replay check the latched clock. The simulator's model had to be extended to read the registers back before the race could be tested (injection at 1,000 points), and a lockstep verifier that feeds port reads from the recording will answer IN 0x253B with a game input unless it models NextREG (Knight Tyme); look for it when logic time drops mid-run.

lessons.title: Without an RZX, compare the patched build against the original in the simulator per path
lessons.text: For Winter Sports (no recording) the patched menu was compared with the original menu loading each of the six events from tape: after 900 frames memory matched outside the hook, system variables and stack, and interrupt mode and flags agreed. The hook also had direct unit tests with a negative control. A free run with scripted keys stands in for a recording (as for Jetpac), but the result is verification without a recording and should be recorded as such.

lessons.title: Keep the original plotter running and remove only its stores: NOP or read instead of write keeps registers, counts, timing and lockstep
lessons.text: Leaving the plotter's save/restore and bookkeeping intact keeps all game state identical to the original, which makes verification simple. Removing only the store instructions kept every register and all timing equal at each frame boundary, except A and F inside loops that follow the bytes read (Pac-Mania, Pyjamarama); instruction count and lockstep stay (Spellbound). A paint store replaced by CP (HL) keeps 7 T and the cell access (a bare NOP made each cell 3 T faster in Sabre Wulf); a copy of a colour paint with the store read instead of written takes the same time to the T-state (Pssst). Chuckie Egg NOPs only the screen pixel and attribute writes; Trueno points the plotter's 'behind the foreground' map at a block of 0xFF so it saves scenery as usual but draws nothing and paints no attribute; a back-buffer game's composing plotter can be changed the same way (swap the figure OR for a background-only load) once the buffer is proven write-first and read only by that plotter. Limit: the removed paint can have been a write the game reads (Starquake's paint ran past the attribute area into 0x5B00, read by collision): save and restore the attributes round the painter and compare against a reference with each frame's paint undone.

lessons.title: Variant builds made by calling an engine's build() directly skip the DivMMC automap-off step that auto adds
lessons.text: The auto command appends z80tonex.automap_off as a last step. Cisco Heat's patch variant script called the engine build directly, so NXC 1.0 shipped without it and also started at 3.5 MHz regardless of player speed. After fixing both and rebuilding, the variants matched the verified build byte for byte. Apply automap_off in any script that bypasses auto.

lessons.title: The nxc harness needs the z80 package, which the shared venv may lack
lessons.text: Abu Simbel: the shared venv has no `z80` package, so the nxc repo's menu tests ran from a private venv. Cisco Heat: on the owner's PC only Python 3.13 has it.

lessons.title: Copy the matching NXC loader with a patch that uses a newer INF1 key; 'Needs this game file' often means an old loader on the card
lessons.text: Copying only a new .nxc to the card left the old /dot/NEXCLASH loader, which read build_screen=nex as an offset 0 and showed the first 6,912 bytes of the game file as the loading screen ('Screen corrupted' on a real Next, R-Type and Castle Master); a correct tape under another name was refused by an old loader from before tape support and any-name detection, and running the card setup script (which replaces only what is out of date) fixed it and confirmed the any-name length scan on real hardware. A loader and a patch format feature (like build_screen) both have to be on the card, or the old behaviour shows with no error. The patch loader finds the game by name first, then by length and MD5. One dot per built bank (up to 24) overran the screen line ('Dots exceed the screen') until the dots were spread over the line width; a short black blink remains between the loader's screen and .nexload because NXCHAND.BAS does a CLS first.

lessons.title: An NXC option set can only change bytes and banks the base build has; plan for 2 MB and reserve banks
lessons.text: R-Type had room for about 98 of an optional intro's 8K pages beside the game in 2 MB while RC1's intro used 196; compressing the pictures only reached 119, storing every 8th of 256 angles (11 degree steps instead of 5.6) fit and made the intro a toggle (limiting tilt was the alternative); the intro sits in banks the game never uses and the option only changes where the stub jumps. For Inferno's English/Czech toggle the two builds differed by only 14 bytes but English had four extra banks, so the base is the English build and the Czech set is the Czech NEX plus those four banks copied unchanged; applying the patch to the tape reproduces the shipped English build byte for byte and the Czech one plus the four banks. In the NXC bank layout SET3 may add only banks 8 and above; Highway Encounter reserved unused 48K banks 6/7 (zero-filled) in the default build so Enhanced can enable Layer 2 pages 12..15 without a format change. A tape without a 6,912-byte screen block cannot use the loading-screen option.

lessons.title: A .z80 snapshot taken after start-up usually no longer holds the loading screen
lessons.text: R-Type's tape loading screen did not appear anywhere in the .z80's eight banks (none of 107 64-byte pieces), because the game had drawn its specification screen over it. So an offset into the player's snapshot cannot supply the screen at ENTER, unlike Castle Master's tape offset. The screen can instead be carried in the .nxc encrypted with a key derived from the player's own game file (build_screen=nex), shown only after the safety check; this worked on a Next for a .z80.

lessons.title: A tape whose data is converted at load cannot be a second .nxc dump target
lessons.text: nxc add-dump accepts another dump (z80, sna, tap, tzx, up to 32) only if it rebuilds the same banks byte for byte, with up to 8 KB of residual bytes carried in the patch. R-Type's tape failed: 79,829 bytes of the snapshot's memory (all eight converted level blocks) were not on the tape, since the loader converts levels as it stores them. Compare the snapshot with the tape in 8-byte pieces first; code blocks matched about 98% but level data only by coincidence. Also, nxc make refuses an output file with data past its banks (950,272 bytes here), so an intro that stores extra data after the banks cannot be a patch.

lessons.title: NXC patches for tape or multiload games: one byte per build option, --start and --tape-bank, loading screen from the tape
lessons.text: Where auto cannot make an NXC patch (tapes, multiloads, build options on the menu), give each build option its own byte so each variant is a valid menu toggle (same length, distinct bytes; Cisco Heat: 25 fps 2 bytes, smooth 1, car 1), verified per variant; use --start and --tape-bank for tape-based games (Cisco Heat took 61,044 bytes from the tape and carried 3,096); point the ENTER loading screen at the tape's SCREEN$ block (build_screen = offset + 3); take cheats from the Spectrum Computing archive, read and test each POKE and leave out ones that do not help the player (Cisco Heat's No Time Bonus was dropped). Verify by rebuilding every option's .nex byte for byte from the patch and the tape, then run the real loader on the Z80 harness; the patch only shows the loading screen at ENTER if the loader includes the preload-screen change. 3D Stock Car: this repo's packager could not make an option needing more memory (SET3) until the re-vendored nxc.py.

lessons.title: NXC format limits: one patch per game, at most 4 toggles, one build_screen offset; unlock time
lessons.text: The project owner stated that a multi-part game such as Winter Sports is one game with one NXC patch: a game-wide colour set and at most 4 toggles shared across every event's plugin, so event-specific extras should go in the colour set, and each option combination must read back exactly to its built NEX. build_screen is one offset (0 to 65535) in the player's file for every target of a patch, naming a 6,912-byte screen, and must sit in the first 252 bytes of menu keys. A 577 KB R-Type .nxc took 2.7 s to unlock at 28 MHz (0.45 s reading the game, 2.3 s checking the patch) and the whole build about 23 s; the preload design absorbs the game and patch in 1K slices while the menu waits for a key so ENTER shows the screen at once.

lessons.title: Get a routine's original time by running it, fit by size
lessons.text: Olli and Lissa derived the routine's time by size and shift by running the routine itself at build time on the snapshot's memory: the hooks came out within 0.01% at the first try once the entry/exit constant was set. New Zealand Story's update fits against the drawing routines' time (residual 0.4 ms of 70) with a simple K plus a constant. Screen contention moves a copy's cost 5% by scene; a fit by rows and columns is unbiased over a stretch and the carry takes up the rest (Nodes of Yesod).

lessons.title: Message screens and full-screen erases wipe figures without the clear routine
lessons.text: A message screen printed over the play area wipes figures without the game's clear routine (Lunar Jetman: find every screen writer per frame and hide sprites there). Dirty rectangles miss a full-screen erase, leaving stale Layer 2 pixels (Movie). Removing a paint can also change logic far away: Lode Runner's editor reads figure attributes on exit, and only a recording of the editor showed it.

lessons.title: Project owner's rule for outline toggles: standard sprites keep the outline, painted sprites default to none
lessons.text: Owner's rule: when the standard colours are used, the outline the build already has stays on by default and an 'Outline off' toggle removes it. When the painted (Enhanced/Spec256) sprite set is chosen, the outline is off by default, and the patch should refuse combining the painted set with an outline toggle that writes the same bytes. Applied to Lunar Jetman, Renegade and Three Weeks. Three Weeks builds patterns at run time, so its outline mode is one hook-page byte (0 own, 1 black, 2 none) and only black, not an arbitrary colour, was possible because every palette entry was in use.

lessons.title: Forward DMA cannot do an overlapping right shift
lessons.text: Bubbler: ordinary forward DMA cannot implement an overlapping right shift directly; copy backward chunks through a dedicated scratch page, or use the verified LDDR fallback.

lessons.title: Overwriters (boxes, wipes, text) make the original leave ghost pixels the patched game will not
lessons.text: When a box or wipe overwrites the figure while it is drawn, the original's later erase leaves ghost pixels; the converted game does not. Differences confined to the undo buffer are fine if nothing else reads it (check references): Magicland had 4 such diffs, Dizzy 6 had 9 and 81. Verify sprite pixels against the screen BEFORE the plot (transparent = unchanged), not against a model, or the ghosts count as mismatches.

lessons.title: Give driver code its own stack when SD or ROM routines run and remap pages
lessons.text: Inferno's first SD auto-save hung the game because the driver's stack disappeared (its page was remapped) while the SD routines ran. The save code now uses its own stack. If hook or driver code calls SD, DOS or ROM routines that change the memory map, put SP somewhere that stays mapped.

lessons.title: Owner rules for added colour: keep shading, start in colour, switchable, fade in colour
lessons.text: The project owner's rules, stated for Castle Master but not game-specific: keep the original's dither shading with colour on top (not flat fills); colour must be switchable off for the original look (done as a palette mapping, so smooth views stay); the game must start in colour, with no visible switch from old look to new; a plain white cursor with no outline that turns dark over light areas. Any user-visible action should be transparent: if colour is added, dissolves play in colour, and a sudden whole-scene change is jarring.

lessons.title: Owner rule: original pace, more views per second, never a faster game
lessons.text: For games where the renderer is sped up, the project owner chose 'original pace, smooth view': the game steps at its original real-time rate and all time the faster renderer saves goes into in-between display views. Faster updates and smaller steps were rejected. Applies to Castle Master and the Hard Drivin' plan.

lessons.title: An aggregate pace number hides opposite errors in quiet and busy scenes, rooms and deaths; report steady drift and bursts separately
lessons.text: Exolon: opposite quiet/busy errors cancel, so keep phase rows and an update-keyed state proof. Dizzy Ultimate: opening-room timing missed a room-transition penalty, so bench room starts separately at the player draw call. Bruce Lee: steady-play averages hid 60-80 ms of extra room-entry time. Booty: a room at 28 MHz needs its original time back (fit over all rooms, then wait at the game's clock). A fixture that starts in a duel or death, or returns to a quiet room, is not a sustained live scene: split windows by actor type or mode (Gunfright, Knight Lore); a +0.16% whole-trial result hid 69-76 ms zone-change penalties and three averages within 2% still held a build (Highway Encounter); measure every room (Herbert: a rare water strip invoked 22 hooks in one room). Report individual slow updates, per-transition timestamps, the steady drift and the largest excursion as separate numbers (Olli and Lissa 3: a steady 0.07% drift was counted as '13 frames ahead'; Starquake's 44 frames against 6 was one sequence with a little slack per iteration, and a hook with no window makes single calls run long and the next windows short). Keep failed trials.

lessons.title: Pace clock readings race with the interrupt; waits and sound ends need the same clock
lessons.text: An interrupt landing between the pace clock's first reading and the 'window open' flag lost a whole frame; the window now opens with interrupts off. A reading taken from game code must be done with interrupts off (or redone if an interrupt came in), and interrupts must always take their own reading. The game's own waits and sound-end loops also have to use the pace clock: 14 real-time waits hooked brought the worst early-ending updates from 6.8 frames early to 0.49 early. Deliberately broken builds for each fix were all rejected.

lessons.title: A debt kept through the menu makes the first updates of play run fast
lessons.text: An ISR hook's cost every frame with no delay to repay it left the first 25 updates of Quazatron run 15% fast; cap the debt at one frame and clear it at the screen clear. Also: a window ticked only at each interrupt, left standing before the ISR's hold, loses a frame when read a whole frame later, and a window that counts only from the ISR hook loses a frame when an interrupt lands in a ROM trampoline: count at every nested hook's close too.

lessons.title: Pace trials need controls and fixtures that keep both runs in lockstep
lessons.text: A 'not measurable' note was the plain control resetting to the menu: a control started from the patch's own start state was in lockstep for 600 updates on every seed (Smash TV). Sabre Wulf's trials drifted apart until every time source of the logic was read from the round counter in both runs; Nodes of Yesod needed the objects' own bytes in the audit's state list, since a time-dependent read in front of a fixed random sequence moves the sequence. Natural encounter divergence is not pace evidence; use controlled fixtures with identical player states over several video phases (Underwurlde). Two pace seeds with identical numbers mean input is not reaching the game (Phantis).

lessons.title: Pace runs must apply input at a point the game reads, not at the frame edge
lessons.text: JNext queues input to the next frame boundary, so an accelerated actor can read a different sample: apply it after the game's read (Alien 8: set A right after the original IN; Father Christmas 8979 after 7E95; Ikari Warriors 0xEB5F; Midnight Resistance), and probe the screen copy because a routine can run twice per update. With many key reads per update apply just before the render (Comando Quatro); Everyone's a Wally Updated had three reads of one row within 2 ms of the probe, so keys given at the game's reads (profile inject) held lockstep; Dizzy Ultimate allows ten idle updates because the first two draws can be under a frame apart. When updates are shorter than a frame, a generator in place of the control read gives both arms the same input (Jilly's Farm); queue replay keys before a long copy window, not at the reader (Herbert); a pace fixture needs R removed and no key waits since input changes only at updates (Mad Mix 2).

lessons.title: Sound or music started by the ISR moves update times: compare sound state or turn music off in both arms
lessons.text: When the ISR plays sound effects, a sound that starts or ends one update apart in two runs moves every update's time by about 50k T for its length (Quazatron), so the pace lockstep must compare the sound variables too. A free-running game with notes played in the ISR compares unlike phases of the tune (Booty: arms a note apart read +13% in a stretch with no real cost): turn music off in both arms for the pace table. Renegade is the other case: a time-slicer game on overrun plays differently, not just slower, so count the game's own skips against the original's as well as the percentage.

lessons.title: Hidden chance sources (R, FRAMES, ROM-read RNG) make two builds play different games: use a test-only fixture in both arms
lessons.text: When the RNG seed advances in the ISR or a wait loop, or LD A,R is read during a HALT, any timing change gives different enemies and the runs diverge: Cobra diverged at update 3; Army Moves and Game Over used BA58 INC HL made NOP in both; Father Christmas made the R reads constant; Abu Simbel an RND-seed fixture; Sabre Wulf draws chance from R in three places and FRAMES in ten (hooks preserve R and pace trials take both out); That Sinking Feeling's ROM-read RNG parted a 128K-ROM game from a Sinclair-ROM build at a spawn; Quazatron's JNext runs of different builds played different games, so pace must be measured update-keyed in lockstep (nexclash.pace), never from free-running logs. Any LD A,R in game logic makes build and original play different games from the first key (Eagle's Nest saw a plain build seem 10,000 T dearer; Lunar Jetman pace by seed varied -25% to +18% over 8 JNext seeds; Gunrunner arms started at another raster phase): make it LD A,I in both test copies (or take R out of the random numbers), or use the replay pace with the recording on both sides as the like-for-like figure, and where code reads R compare with the original IRQ at the same game instruction. Apply the same fixture to original and build and cover every R read: Comando Quatro's full-snapshot scan found a third LD A,R the first list missed.

lessons.title: Whether a game needs a pace limiter, and which scheme, depends on how it syncs
lessons.text: A game that waits on its own interrupts needs no K window on the update; 28 MHz to the wait is enough and fine windows only add cost (Eagle's Nest; likewise a game with its own frame sync and idle time at the end of the update, Commando). A game held by HALTs only needs its time right at the frame edge, so plots at 28 MHz need no window (Father Christmas, lockstep at 25 a second). A game with no frame sync and a hook cost per draw needs no limiter: run a fixed stretch of the same draw's set-up at 28 MHz (Jetpac). A flat-out game with no frame wait needs a K window round all it can, since every hook entry at 3.5 MHz is its own cost (Jilly's Farm). A CPU-bound game whose hooks cost more than the original's idle time can still be paced by running one of its own long routines at 28 MHz (Cyclone's 38 ms renderer: +15% to within 1%; the earlier 'a limiter cannot make a slow build faster' was wrong).

lessons.title: Where a hook's time can be repaid
lessons.text: Time can be repaid only where the original wastes some: a delay the game pads each pass with (Solomon's Key pads to ten figures' time, so repayment to the T-state gave +0.1% against +2.1%; Quazatron's delay scales with droid count and vanishes at 6+ blocks, so it must be repaid), a fixed-length LDIR/LDDR scroll move in uncontended RAM (exact original time), the game's own 21 ms scroll run at 28 MHz (Scooby-Doo), or a fixed-time plot following the game's sync (Starquake). A frame-locked game waiting on FRAMES needs no limiter round its plots (Page Pharaoh). Contended screen writes are not exact enough.

lessons.title: Predicting an update's original duration: cycles plus contention, measured with a cycle timer
lessons.text: For a game with no frame wait, an update's real time fitted as CPU T-states (game plus ISR) plus about 1.23 T per access to 0x4000-0x7FFF: 99.9% of test updates within 2%, median error 0.14% (Castle Master, 5,379 updates). A pacer on the Next that uses a cycle timer plus per-call savings and hook counters reached 96% within 2%; counters alone gave a 7% median error, so a timer is needed. Frames Fuse writes for an interrupt that was held off are near-empty (about 20 T) and must be counted by their actual T, not as whole frames, or about 146 updates look one frame short.

lessons.title: A pace window longer than a frame loses whole frames unless the clock or debt is ticked inside it
lessons.text: A debt or hold window that spans a frame wrap loses the lines of the lost frame: Mad Mix 2 lost 311 lines so the wait ran a frame long (K tuning hid it); Midnight Resistance lost whole frames on a commit over 20 ms until hlib_pace_tick ran per figure; Gunfright had to tick before a frame could wrap; Cyclone's 35 ms hook ticked once measured +8.8% and ticking after each long step gave +0.3%; Everyone's a Wally Updated lost a whole frame (21 ms) on each early update to a commit inside a window; Gauntlet's full-screen pass ran 70,000 T too long until it read the clock every row; Atom Ant without hlib_debt_tick lost a whole frame of debt in one nest and ran 36% slow (found by timing the hook's parts). Knight Lore's multi-frame hold needs bounded chunks with checkpoints. Jilly's Farm: the debt cap also applies inside a window, so capping it low stops nested work counting; trim or bank what is left after the wait. A fixed-looking +20 ms at one update reads as this wrap, not a slow hook.

lessons.title: Forcing 60 Hz speeds a frame-interrupt-paced game up by about 20%; keep original speed by pacing from the CTC
lessons.text: If a game's speed comes from the frame interrupt (Inferno's pacing routine waits for the next interrupt), running at 60 Hz makes gameplay about 20% faster, shortens frames so the hooks get less time, and shortens sounds that play in the slack. Keeping original speed on a 60 Hz display would need pacing from the CTC instead of the frame interrupt, a larger change with possible judder. This was reasoned, not tested.

lessons.title: A 7FFD write (game, ISR or level unpack) resets MMU slots and can map ROM over the slot holding hook code, page or stack
lessons.text: R-Type's level unpacker writes port 7FFD, which on the Next maps ROM over the MMU slot that held the hook code; the next interrupt ran into ROM and reset to NextZXOS (an earlier diagnosis, the game's load check, was wrong and patching bank 0 is fine; builds tested only from mid-level snapshots missed it, so test a full start and a level change; the fix puts the code back straight after the unpack, and stopping on the paging-port write in a debugger shows the slot mapping). An IM 2 handler that writes 7FFD resets MMU 0, 1, 6 and 7 (Lode Runner), so a hook window into another bank must use another slot; Head Over Heels' writes replace MMU1 so a private stack there is lost while a stack in a spare page in MMU2 survived; Eagle's Nest crashed when a wrapper mapped slot 1 to ROM while the hook stack was in slot 1 (restore what was found, not an assumed state); the original ISR may leave bank 1 selected, so an interrupt check must start from the recording's current 7FFD. Cisco Heat: a 7FFD write inside w_go (paging bank 1) put ROM back into MMU slot 0 so a save went to ROM and the restore read ROM (51 characters printed for 18, updates 3 frames long), and paging for the in-between frames swapped the Next's ROM back in, garbling messages and making each update 3 frames too long: model the reset in the verifier and check ROM and paging state at every entry and exit of added drawing code. Castle Master: setup_call runs with the stub in slots 6-7, so a write to the game's 0xC000-0xFFFF there lands in the stub's bank (only JNext showed it): put start-up state in the image.

lessons.title: Painting sheet rules stated by the owner for sprites and scenery
lessons.text: Owner's rules for R-Type painting sheets: list each unique sprite once (a shared COMMON sheet for figures drawn identically in several levels, per-level sheets only for figures that differ in colour or are enemies), group look-alike sprites together, put ship, laser, Force pod and collectable groups together on COMMON, and keep enemies on the level sheet where they first appear with a keep list for exceptions. Scenery sheets are keyed by distinct 8x8 cell content, so painting one cell colours every place it is used. Sheet changes alter layout only and need no rebuild test.

lessons.title: Check a palette's origin before committing it, and what a palette check really reads
lessons.text: Army Moves: the Spec256-Games palette committed as a profile was byte for byte the one Booty and Lunar Jetman keep out of the repo (licence not established); keep it a local MD5-pinned input. Alien 8: palette_check reads tables, not draws, flagging 4 default entries the build never draws (figures use entries 64 + ink); check the indices drawn before claiming a shade is seen. Cookie: palette_wrong replays the boot's NEXTREG writes against the painted map, since fixed colours compared only as symbols missed the real RGB.

lessons.title: Fix sprite-pattern cache churn with LRU eviction, a real per-update budget, and slots for non-empty tiles only
lessons.text: In R-Type, when conversion could not keep up the code fell back to the game's ULA drawing and figures showed as 8x8 attribute blocks. Causes fixed: a budget bug (the first conversion each update zeroed the 24-tile budget, so one new figure per update), a full cache restart whenever the 128 patterns filled or eviction that could drop entries in use (replaced by least-recently-used eviction that never evicts an entry stamped this update), and big graphics needing one unbroken run of slots sized to their whole outline (now only non-empty tiles are reserved, failures 51 to 0). Level 1 fallbacks went from 294 to 0 (levels 2 and 4-7 had none); level 3's battleship (about 180 patterns) still overflowed the 128 patterns (a budget of 72 did not help) and more than 128 hardware sprites in one update also occurred once (an explosion). Cache size was shrunk several times to make code room without measuring its effect in busy scenes.

lessons.title: Sprite checks that compare x, y and pattern number miss bad pattern data
lessons.text: 34 patterns are 8,704 bytes: the upload ran off an 8K page and the last two objects were noise in both modes, yet every test passed because the sprite checks compare x, y and pattern number, not the pattern (That Sinking Feeling). A side-by-side with the set found it; the upload needs its own check against the art.

lessons.title: Per-update pattern building and upload can cost more than the displaced routine
lessons.text: Building 4-bit patterns from game bytes at run time (two table lookups a byte) cost 113 T a byte at 28 MHz, more than the displaced routine when the picture changes every pass: made once and kept in spare pages, then OTIR, the pace came out within 0.07% (Olli and Lissa 3). Per-update uploads of about 20k T overran Quazatron's 33-66k T delay: an image-keyed cache came before any limiter tuning. A colour animation re-converts the image every 4 frames (Spellbound): the miss cost sets the pace, not the hit rate.

lessons.title: Per-screen tables cost an 8K page each; an unexpanded Next has about 95 pages
lessons.text: Trueno stored one 8K Layer 2 table page per screen (pages 60-83 used), and sprite patterns for 1378 figures took 22 pages, moving Layer 2 to other banks. Plan memory before adding per-screen data and pack several screens per page if more places come.

lessons.title: Cached per-graphic pixel lists beat recomputing, and replaying the list beats clearing a rectangle
lessons.text: Flying Shark at 28 MHz: cached pixel lists beat recomputing rings by a factor of 7, and clearing by replaying the list beat clearing a rectangle.

lessons.title: POKE cheats that change game logic keep working after the display is replaced; display POKEs do not
lessons.text: Tipshop POKEs for R-Type matched this snapshot's addresses. Infinite lives, immunity, invincibility and the attachments key worked in CSpect because the original logic still runs; 'remove background scenery' had no effect because Layer 2 draws the scenery rather than the game's own code. Test each cheat, and match POKE addresses to the exact version before shipping them.

lessons.title: Port 0x303B is shared by the sprite attribute index and the pattern upload index; Copper timing and palette facts from CSpect
lessons.text: An interrupt that updates sprite attributes and main code that uploads patterns both use port 0x303B, so the ISR moving sprites garbled uploads in progress (R-Type): the interrupt stays off it while patterns upload or the main code is in glide code, counts the steps it skipped and the main code makes them up afterwards (keep update lengths even). In CSpect, a Copper WAIT on line n at h 40 took effect from Layer 2 row n + 32 of the 320x256 layer; the Copper restarts at vertical blank after the top-border lines (280 to 311), so the top band's palette must be set at the end of the previous frame; 9-bit palette writes (NR 0x44 pairs) did not work from the Copper while 8-bit NR 0x41 writes did. The Copper facts were seen in CSpect, not confirmed on hardware.

lessons.title: Porting an engine by matching bytes finds sites, not their spans or new readers
lessons.text: Arc of Yesod: the copy hook's exit was one instruction short (the loop's own JP), seen only as R one out; compare each site's whole original span. Once a paint stops writing the screen, every reader of what it wrote must be found (scan the screen's readers), not only the ones the model engine hooks.

lessons.title: A 128K game writing port 0xFF scrambles the picture on a Next
lessons.text: A 128K game can write port 0xFF for no reason a 128K sees; on a Next that selects Timex hi-colour and scrambles the picture (Mad Mix 2). Found by looking at the plain conversion's JNext screen, not by any check: grep OUT (0xFF) in a plain conversion before designing.

lessons.title: Generalised probes exist: routine_skip and pacing_census
lessons.text: The kept probes take the game's addresses as arguments. routine_skip replays each update with one CALL skipped, feeding recorded inputs, LD A,R values and interrupts, then compares game RAM; pacing_census reports time and frames per update, slack before the next frame, who calls the frame wait and every beeper OUT. On Chuckie Egg skipping the attribute refresh left 133 of 133 updates identical and skipping the hens differed every update (the negative control). Without recorded R values Inferno level 6 diverges, as expected.

lessons.title: Profile per routine and count calls before estimating a gain, optimising or assigning cost
lessons.text: Castle Master: two early estimates were wrong (the view copy was called about half of a view's cost but ran once per update, 3%; a 5-8% blitter gain became 1-3% since the clear was 2% of an average update); no hot spot existed (largest routine 13%, geometry 27-34%, raster about 31%), and the +12% views came from the divide, row set-up, a DMA view copy and not idling before in-between flips. Atic Atac: profile a hook by the lines one call takes (a JDS rule at entry and return); build at 257 to 297 lines a call was hidden by the audit's per-update hook times. Atom Ant: timing the hook's parts, not reasoning, found the lost debt. Per-routine T from the assembler symbols showed bookkeeping and attribute writes, not the guessed uploads, as the next costs (Lunar Jetman); misses are the cost of an image cache (38 ms against 0.1 in Ikari Warriors): count them per update; a hook run for every object each update cost about 7% against 2-6% for hooks that switch speed (Lunar Jetman): count calls per update and skip when state says nothing to do. Profile complete hooks before blaming large copies (Highway Encounter); require one timing row per hook so an empty list cannot look like success (Inferno).

lessons.title: Prove free memory (hook tails, start-up code) with an access scan over every stage and recording: untouched is not free
lessons.text: Untouched may only mean 'room not visited', so also require zero content for persistent code, and scan every wave, room and stage before choosing a tail: the survey's 'free RAM' means untouched by that recording (Atic Atac 0xB536-, 0xD2EE-: graphics never drawn); 0x9000-0x901F looked free in wave 1 and took writes in other waves (Silkworm); room 0's free memory held other rooms' data (Solomon's Key: tail moved to write-first memory proven on all rooms); art mapped in slot 2 hid a room map below 0x6000 (Ruff and Reddy: read the game's data before mapping over it); Comando Quatro's 5B10 looked untouched over 2,500 frames and was first read later; Green Beret's 0x9400 looked untouched until the fourth stage; Auf Wiedersehen Monty's converter guess landed in composite cells and only the ROM path check (reads before writes) caught it; a test state saved in play has a room in the buffer where a tail would draw a line (Three Weeks, test builds only). The printer buffer is not always free (Dizzy 1 keeps its stack above it, Magicland a bit-reverse table, Rainbow code, Wally uses 0x5B00-0x7AFF, Trueno uses it), and below-SP default placement can hit data (Dizzy 1 font at 0xFF9E) or code (Magicland). Strongest tail sites: printer buffer never touched, an undo or back buffer written before read in every RZX, dead stack, bytes whose first access is a write; confirm over the longest recordings and every stage, and prove per release snapshot (a snapshot taken mid-routine needs its own tail proof).

lessons.title: Screen publication and flips tear depending on beam phase; sweep the phase
lessons.text: A flip while the copy ends with the beam in the window's upper rows tears; put it at the copy's start with the beam below the window and the opaque picture hides the copy (Mad Mix 2). Flush queued scenery before the final border wait; a large flush inside the sprite publication window can push attribute writes into active display, and a faster renderer can make a caught unsafe-publication negative pass at one phase (Herbert: sweep raster phases, good build passes all, broken one fails where publication reaches display).

lessons.title: A published or approved build must be reproducible from the engine alone, not from run-folder post-steps
lessons.text: Published and approved builds repeatedly relied on steps outside the engine (derived start state, loading-screen step, add_screen, Enhanced colour map, v1.0 stub / v2.10 fix-up, byte transplant, recolour(), run-folder scripts): Commando (clean_start, loading_nex), Dizzy Ultimate, Everyone's a Wally Updated (to128, loading_nex, Enhanced map), Atic Atac (v1.3 delta scripts), Nightshade, Rambo, Renegade, Smash TV, Starquake, Target Renegade, New Zealand Story, Jetpac v1.1 (recolour() and a loading-screen stub), Ikari Warriors (default route changed; the recolour guard caught a stale check), Knight Tyme (loading screen as a post-step script). They now run inside auto so main reproduces the published MD5s. An import compares against nxc.py --bare, not the record (Rambo's record outputs were stale), and moves each step into build()/auto with its stub source in the engine's .asm, the screen taken from the tape beside the snapshot and a model run of the stub; keep private-input builds as separately named commands (Knight Lore). A published build carried onto an older one and patched is not main's build. Reserved-bank defaults also drifted: Game Over's constant for a build without sets (83) was above the real top (75), Army Moves 1.1 needed reserve=True, and Chase H.Q.'s published alt ROM banks were 45/44 not 47/46.

lessons.title: Python and path pitfalls on Windows
lessons.text: Python 3.14's forkserver needs a main guard and dead-register subprocesses an explicit fork context (Underwurlde); a venv must be called by its absolute path or Python warns about sys.prefix, and a relative run path made JNext miss the card copy (Silkworm: byte_exact False showed it). sjasmplus warns on backslashes in the source path (forward slashes fixed it, profiles identical) and sjasm.py could not find or build the pinned assembler on Windows (Rainbow Islands engine). An autocrlf checkout on Windows failed 18 doc size budgets (Trap Door).

lessons.title: Random numbers drawn from an address built from R read any byte of memory
lessons.text: A game that draws random numbers from a byte at an address made of R can read any byte of memory: removing figures from a buffer or screen, or changing any byte of a patched site (no changed byte at an address of form A*257 in Heartland), alters the game. Heartland's first design passed every per-hook picture check and failed only the whole-state comparison 906 steps in. A hook wrapping such a routine must hand it the original's R (not only leave the original's R after), and changing the data it works on can change its instruction count, so R needs a correction per case. A unit case forcing each branch finds this; recordings take only the plain path.

lessons.title: Per-hook R checks do not prove the global R trajectory
lessons.text: Bruce Lee: per-hook native R checks passed while the original idle/IRQ phase changed global R and some random decisions. Bubbler: a death HALT's fetch-count difference (6,459 mod 128) explains the full R offset 59; separate that from hook R correctness. Exolon: moving the speed latch before the IFF/R capture needs R corrected for the 15 fetches moved. Dizzy Ultimate: the inherited comparison excluded R and including it exposed differences at seven hook sites. Beyond the Ice Palace: particle and damage routines need R preserved even inside rendering. Gryzor: a star hook that works out the original's bytes from the plot list keeps R exact with no fixture.

lessons.title: Reach hard-to-reach game states with pokes or saved cheat-run snapshots
lessons.text: Dynamite Dan: poke the start room to reach every room cheaply; a per-room census found the sinking code that a no-cheat recording never reached, but it counts Dan spawned inside scenery, so use play recordings for clash numbers and the census for coverage (bot rollouts got stuck in room 6). Altered Beast: a cheat-run state saved as .z80 and built as a test .nex put the boss on screen in JNext in seconds. Green Beret: poking 0xFFDF after start reaches a later stage.

lessons.title: Rebuild from the record after the final tuning change
lessons.text: Abu Simbel's record and notes kept the K 111 build's MD5 after K went to 100; only rebuilding against the published patch found it. Rebuild and re-stamp after the last change, not before.

lessons.title: The shared recorder, analyse, verify and new paths are 48K only; 128K engines carry their own copies
lessons.text: nexclash.py record and analyse drive a 48K machine and paging is not in machine.py: 128K recordings used the pilot's private m128.py (7FFD paging, banks in save/load; replays cleanly through rzxplay), and Exolon's 48K-only recorder failed before producing a recording. nexclash/verify.py is 48K-only (list memory), so 128K engines carry a copy (Fantasy World Dizzy's fwd128, Treasure Island Dizzy's tid128; Pac-Mania's verifier needed its own 128K paging, a flat view plus banks swapped on 7FFD); nexclash.py new stopped on a 128K snapshot with the 48K-only analysis (Simpsons: work went on with scan, isr, preview and a trace script).

lessons.title: A game that compares whole port values ignores every key if the recorder returns 0xFF on port FE
lessons.text: `record` returned 0xFF on port FE and Abu Simbel ignored every key with no warning; an Issue 3 recorder (floating-bus bits) fixed it. Check that scripted keys visibly move the player before trusting a recording.

lessons.title: Auto-recorder: match rooms by similarity and reset per-segment state
lessons.text: Matching rooms by exact attribute hash made moving objects into fake rooms (Dizzy V's bubbles trapped the explorer); matching with <=25% of cells differing fixed it. Honest room counts stayed at 1-4 in 6,000-60,000 frames, so the explorer does not solve puzzles and a short human RZX gives better coverage. The recorder writes one RZX segment per episode and rzxplay builds a new Simulator per segment, so any sync state must reset in __init__ (stale screen model gave false refusals a few frames after a segment start).

lessons.title: Recorded inputs alone miss errors in a bit-exact port: use random and edge sweeps and deliberately broken builds
lessons.text: Castle Master: replacements checked only on recorded inputs can pass wrongly (two of four broken multiply/divide variants passed every recorded call and were caught only by random inputs, edge values and the full 8x8 input space); a stage missed in a port (an off-screen sector cull, 0x8D4F) showed as one wrong cube in one of 5,233 redraws, so run every redraw, not a sample. Gate stage by stage at fixed PCs with a failing mutant each, then end to end; keep a set of mutants (rounding, sign swap, missing hook) and require all to be rejected; keep random sweeps in the inputs' domain (beyond it failures are false); a mutant can be equivalent, so replace it; a control that saves, clobbers, then restores is no control, and one on a rare path needs its own direct check.

lessons.title: One recording per game that follows the checklist: start at the title, play long, replay whole, and check what it covers
lessons.text: A recording of 3-5 minutes should start the game, cross 6-8 rooms, use items and inventory, hit dialogue and a lost life, stand next to moving things and revisit a room; render the recording's contact sheet to see what it contains. A recording that starts mid-game leaves the sprite and figure models empty while the screen has figures (Lunar Jetman: start at the title with cheats poked into the start state). Chuckie Egg's RZX covered levels 1-2 only (no lifts, no free duck) and Rainbow's covered no later islands (banks 3/4/6 never paged), so code reached only there is proven by unit tests, not replay. Owner play of four minutes gave 2,485 game steps and the bolt where six scripted recordings gave about 550 steps each and no bolt (Heartland); a recording ending at 16% is not completion (Movie); a verify capped at 6,000 frames missed more than a whole replay (Lode Runner); per-level replays found a canvas-clear bug the shorter recording passed (Gunrunner). Slice an InputRecording by each frame's start and end since its data includes frame headers (Jet Set Willy); a search bot must restore its start state on failure or the script no longer replays.

lessons.title: Make recordings honestly, and read the right bank
lessons.text: A game's own debug or room skip reaches far rooms honestly (Prince of the Yolkfolk: C + direction held until the room changes, a SPACE tap to leave) but skipping past the last room crashes into ROM and poisons every later scan (Solomon's Key: read the level count first). A 128K snapshot pages bank 3 at C000, so a dump from C000 up shows the player's bank, not the game's (Ruff and Reddy, wrong bytes at first).

lessons.title: A recording that starts from another state fools the tail and ROM path check
lessons.text: Flying Shark: a fixture recording that starts after the unpack holds game data where the build's start-up tail sits, so the ROM path check reports tail reads the real start never makes; replay such fixtures by hand and keep verify-list recordings starting from the snapshot. Arc of Yesod: nextboot.rom_paths treats a recording that starts elsewhere as starting at the build's snapshot, so a tail in write-first memory is reported as read.

lessons.title: Replace the picture rather than recognising it from the pixels the original drew
lessons.text: R-Type's first route let the original draw into its buffer and then re-identified every 8x8 cell and rebuilt sprite patterns each update; even with the main loop at 28 MHz that took about 93% of the time, busy updates took 4-6 frames, it could not use hardware scrolling, and the picture still moved exactly as the original copier moved it, with clipping and flicker. The route that worked keeps the original logic running hidden, draws scenery on Layer 2 moved by the hardware scroll register and picks ready-made sprite patterns by which graphic the game asks to draw. The original scrolled one pixel per game update (about 16 a second at best), so hardware scrolling makes it even but not 50 Hz.

lessons.title: Replace a plotter outright when it reads only its graphics and a back buffer the game never reads
lessons.text: Everyone's a Wally: convert the graphics straight to patterns and emulate the plotter's end state (alternate registers, flags via the same OR/ADD, stack PUSH, self-modified operands). Simpler than Rainbow's canvas runs and verified exact. Re-run a plotter at its REAL address with a RAM page mapped over the screen when you do run it; re-basing DE to a private canvas broke plotters that save D, run leftwards or are 6 bytes wide.

lessons.title: A recording that loses sync must count as a failure, and start-up must keep the player's CPU speed
lessons.text: When nexclash main tightened its engine rules, two real defects in Cisco Heat were caught: a replay that lost sync was counted as a pass, and the start-up code forced 3.5 MHz instead of keeping the speed the player had chosen. Check that verification fails on desync, and that start-up code restores or keeps the CPU speed setting.

lessons.title: Check which palette indices are really transparent before remapping
