lessons.text: In Head Over Heels index 255 is painted white, not free transparency: reserve an exact duplicate and remap only at the final copy, keep source mask values untouched, and reset the ULA bright-black entry when global transparency changes. Highway Encounter's supplied .pal is 256 text RGB triplets, not raw bytes: assert count and dimensions in the decoder.

lessons.title: Verify a long routine from its RET state
lessons.text: To verify a hook on a long routine, start from the original's state at its RET (full runs for the first 20 calls): full verify took 14 minutes instead of hours (Nemesis).

lessons.title: A reused builder variable wrote startup code over the bank loader and caused a restart on every level load
lessons.text: In Inferno's English build a reused variable in the ROM builder wrote the English startup code over the bank loader, so the first level load restarted the game and brought back the Kempston question. The user's exact key sequence reproduced it, and my scripted typing had hidden it because letters were dropped. Build tools should check that no two ROM regions overlap.

lessons.title: Graphics the game rewrites in place cannot have pre-built patterns or cached tables
lessons.text: Arc of Yesod: scan the graphics for writers before trusting a catalogue of patterns. Booty: a table by the graphic's address is right only while the bytes never change (the replay's ULA check found it in 500 frames). Cookie: a copy of a routine the game rewrites keeps the bytes it was assembled with; where every caller wants the change, edit the one instruction in place.

lessons.title: At the right edge the ULA wraps an overflowing byte, a sprite clips
lessons.text: A plotter that writes past column 31 wraps into the next row (INC E / INC HL) where a hardware sprite clips. Classify these unit-test cases as 'not a game case' when the recordings never reach them, and let any real occurrence with pixels fail the RZX pixel check. Seen in Rainbow (6-wide piece at column >= 27), Chuckie Egg (player/duck x > 240, hens x = 248).

lessons.title: A static ROM read mismatch is not automatically a consumed value
lessons.text: Exolon: B0B7's original self-copy LDIR is a delay, so reading ROM bytes there consumes nothing. Keep a per-read guard and a full-function ABI/time proof before exempting 2000..3FFF; never broadly waive unknown ROM consumers or final flags.

lessons.title: A recording with test pokes keeps sync if each poke starts a new segment
lessons.text: A recording with test pokes stays in sync when each poke starts a new segment from its own snapshot; rom_paths reports this in its lines.

lessons.title: The 128K ROM 1 differs from the 48K ROM (keypad code at 0x386E); recordings may desync
lessons.text: The 128K ROM 1 differs from Sinclair's 48K ROM in keypad code (29 MISMATCH reads in Lode Runner when 48K ROM was used for a ROM 1 image; the fade reads every ROM byte). In Knight Tyme 128-1.rom has keypad code at 0x386E on the ISR path and a stub there broke replay; recordings made on the 48K ROM desynced the 128K run at frame 2. rom_paths tries 48K ROM as ROM 1 and per segment, and a record's rom_paths_known lists known differences (Bridge star map reads the Next's ROM 0 at 0x0D00-0x0D20, 33 bytes seen).

lessons.title: In-between frames by running the next update ahead with partial movement and restoring every byte it changed
lessons.text: Cisco Heat's smooth engine runs each real update at 28 MHz, waits until the original would have finished, then in the spare time saves the write set, runs the next update ahead with only part of its movement, shows that picture and puts back every byte the update changed so the game state is untouched. Checked exact in 159 of 159 recording cases (511 extra frames, none late), 400 more saved states and 754 frames in the final build. The in-between frame can only start early in a frame and the deadline check must count that wait (one frame finished 59 lines past its deadline until fixed); at 50 fps each in-between frame needed about 383 lines of work, more than one 311-line frame, so about 25 pictures a second was the practical limit. One game only, not confirmed on hardware or by a second game.

lessons.title: RZX facts for tools: compressed SPIN snapshots, zeroed T, fetch-count frames, short interrupt frames
lessons.text: SPIN RZX snapshot blocks are zlib-compressed (flag 2) (Nemesis; nexclash.py rzx extract now reads them). rzxplay zeroes T before next_frame, so a verifier's frame T lost every RZX frame a game frame spanned and 'frames over 20 ms' read too low (13 vs 2 in the first 2000 frames of one game); the beam must be one monotonic formula. Frames by RZX fetch count stay aligned when hooks run in ROM and each site keeps its fetch count (Pac-Mania; Rambo: fetch counts keep interrupt-driven music in step where T-state frames do not). Fuse writes a short frame of about 20 T when an interrupt delayed by DI lands, so a frame count runs ahead of real time; weigh short frames by their T (Castle Master).

lessons.title: Count hits of key routines in the recordings to learn the game's lifecycle before changing it
lessons.text: Counting hits of routine addresses in Inferno's RZX files showed the level block was set up once while play started four times from the copy already in memory, and gameplay exited four times. That proved the original does no reload on a retry, so skipping the sprite rebuild on a same-level retry matches it. Limits: it did not say why each exit happened, and recordings that start after loading never ran the level or story steps.

lessons.title: An RZX carries its own start snapshot, so an RZX alone is a complete intake; check it before planning
lessons.text: Run rzxinfo first: an RZX holds the snapshot it was recorded from, so intake can start from the RZX alone (nexclash.py rzx extract R -o GAME.z80); the RECORDING_CHECKLIST gained a line saying so, and a plain NEX may then need a start address in memory the recording never touches (Hard Drivin' used 0x6C00; a full-length survey of 167,135 frames replayed without losing sync). Atic Atac took the .z80's loader state for the recording's and planned an unneeded prerun. The embedded snapshot can be a different build than the delivered .z80 (Cauldron: 11,283 bytes, code shifted; Alien 8: it differed from the repo's reference so recorded output MD5s cannot match), which the survey does not yet compare. A snapshot taken in play can make a fixed-length table scan misread: Alien 8's reader scanned 256 table words and four words past the real table parsed as graphics (nexclash crashed with 'not the Alien 8 graphic table'); stopping where the first graphic begins fixed it. A re-saved tape whose BASIC loader POKEs different bytes will not match the engine's accepted tape hash, so no loading screen is taken from it.

lessons.title: A write census over the first 2,000 frames can falsely show a table is never written; run censuses over whole recordings
lessons.text: In Inferno a 2,000-frame sample showed nothing writing the tile graphics area (so a change-counter cache looked safe), but the full recordings showed each level's own code rewriting tiles partway through (level 3 also a second range). The cheap change-counter validation was dropped and exact byte comparison kept. Run write and read censuses over whole recordings before building a cache or invalidation scheme on a 'never written' result.

lessons.title: Rendering in a copy of memory: redirect the interrupt to the real memory
lessons.text: If extra views are rendered by the game's own code inside a paged copy of memory for 100 ms or more, the game's interrupt handler must still run on the real memory or its real-time clocks slow down. A small stub in a slot the renderer never touches (here the ROM slot, unused by the game) can save SP, switch to its own stack in an unused RAM area, map the real pages, call the handler, then map the copy back. It cost 245 T per interrupt and passed all 79,705 recorded interrupts in the simulator (negative controls: no remap, one slot unmapped, SP not restored all failed). Only simulator-tested; the handler's R-based random delays differed in 229 bytes (cosmetic here).

lessons.title: A render in a memory copy must read some state live and draw over the last frame
lessons.text: Re-running the game's renderer in a copy matched the game's own frame on 5,202 of 5,214 redraws; the other 12 had two causes. A counter the ISR decrements mid-render (it picked the sky/ground split) must be read from the real memory, not the copy. The renderer also does not rebuild its buffer fully (fills read and modify bytes, the clear misses some), so the copy must start from the last frame shown: a test that pre-filled the buffer with junk failed almost everywhere and was a false alarm. Panel and screen writes in the render path must not reach the real screen, and any bytes the render leaves for game logic (Hard Drivin' leaves 23) must be saved and restored around extra views, drawing the real view last.

lessons.title: Scripted keys are often missed or mean something unexpected: check the key decoder, menu timing and pause keys, and that the player really moves
lessons.text: Check that scripted keys visibly move the player: Commando's published +0.38% used keys the game never reads; Exolon's decoder (Z/X stationary, O/P worked); Dizzy Ultimate: P pauses this release; Scooby-Doo: J opens a joystick menu where K picks Kempston, so a script holding Kempston directions looks like it plays while nothing moves, and ENTER landing while a joystick menu closes spoiled the first pace run; Three Weeks: 3 selects keyboard and toggles Wally's colour; Fantasy World Dizzy: an ENTER tap opened the inventory (release held keys and key to the game's own input poll). Menus poll from the interrupt every few frames or run long routines, so short pulses are missed (Phantis J press; Gryzor 1-frame JNext press missed in the original too: hold the key; Gunfright six-frame pulses missed a long beeper routine and a 350-frame press worked), while held keys can step past the end of a letter wheel (Father Christmas: short presses with waits) and a start key still held when play begins reads as input (Page Pharaoh). Titles may need a key sequence: Comando Quatro takes a key only after its tune started; Gunrunner needs one key to pass the picture then one to pick controls; Mad Mix 2's READY wait wants all keys up first; a loading screen shifts input timing (Head Over Heels: anchor startup keys to the entry PC and assert real player updates before a long soak) and pokes applied after the start key miss the test level (Gunrunner). A tune without interrupts tests keys only between notes (Solomon's Key); OverSpec resumes a game's last session from its data folder (use a fresh folder; Olli and Lissa) and its scripted keys reach it only while its window has focus (Olli and Lissa 3). Check the game really changed.

lessons.title: Update hardware scroll and sprites together, once per update, after the raster leaves the play area
lessons.text: In the R-Type hybrid the Layer 2 scroll position and the sprite attributes are written in one step, waiting until the raster is below the play area, which removes tearing between scenery and figures (before this they changed at different moments and the picture could lag one update). Normally an update starts just after the frame interrupt, so the wait only occurs after a slow update.

lessons.title: z88dk 2.5 / zsdcc facts checked for the +zxn target
lessons.text: __sdcccall(1) functions clean the stack themselves only if non-variadic and returning void or 16 bits or less; otherwise the caller cleans. Do not use -Cs"--sdcccall 1" globally: it links but calls library helpers such as __mullong with register args while the library takes stack args, so results are garbage; use __sdcccall(1) per function. With sdcc_iy asm may clobber AF, BC, DE, HL and IY (IX must be kept; the ROM IM1 handler expects IY = 0x5C3A); the IY part was read from the config, not tested. For a .nex, appmake needs __register_sp and an entry address symbol unless --nex-norun is used, and a section named BANK_n, PAGE_n etc. is placed in its bank, while BANK_5, BANK_2 and BANK_0 merge into main memory and an overlapping section aborts the build. A global initialised to 0 still goes to data_compiler.

lessons.title: selftest and re-verify need the game's reference files, so some games cannot be re-verified on a given PC
lessons.text: Alien 8, Heartland, Gauntlet and Arc of Yesod could not be re-verified (selftest --game, selftest --verify --stamp) on one PC because their reference files were not in the local specnext checkout; merges then rely on contributors' stamps plus doccheck and CI. State this in the PR rather than implying it was checked.

lessons.title: A selftest that skips a game because its recording is missing prints PASSED but proves nothing
lessons.text: With the reference recording absent, selftest --game <name> printed 'SELFTEST PASSED for the games run (1 skipped)'. The game had not been verified at all; only a boot check in the emulator was possible. Read the skipped count, and say a build is unverified when the replay did not run. Related: a full selftest run can hit a time-out on another game and never reach the one you changed.

lessons.title: Per-redraw tests miss what happens between redraws; test the whole sequence
lessons.text: Overlay hooks that passed every per-redraw check still failed on hardware: the cursor moves between redraws and the interrupt-driven printer writes to the view buffer between views without reaching the screen. A test replaying the build's overlay code along the whole recording (5,357 views, 3,670 cursor moves) would have caught it. Also, byte-granular 'screen differs from buffer' rules turn a 1-pixel crosshair into a whole opaque block; make an overlay sprite opaque only where the screen differs from what the renderer drew, with the marker excluded from that reference.

lessons.title: Serpentine plotters store alternate rows reversed, so in-place shifts go opposite ways on odd rows
lessons.text: Rainbow Islands stores alternate rows of the player graphics reversed because its plotters draw serpentine. When the game shifts the player in place, odd rows move the opposite way in memory to even rows, so a sheet that maps a shifted pixel back to its unshifted source must un-shift by row parity. Treating all rows as forward made some pixels ink in one figure and clear in another and landed painted colours in the wrong places. A probe that un-shifted 444,840 player rows from two recordings showed 0 mismatches with the parity rule; the sheet command now reports such conflicts.

lessons.title: A setup text substitution can silently miss; check actual layer opacity
lessons.text: Gunfright's Enhanced setup substitution silently missed because of different leading whitespace, leaving black as transparent; checking pattern indices did not show it, but compositing the real palette/attributes/patterns exposed 122 lost ink pixels. Check the full-layer result after a scripted edit and keep the old build as the negative.

lessons.title: Objects drawn into a scrolling back buffer become sprites through a shadow map kept by hooks
lessons.text: Rainbow's collectables are tile cells in the scrolling background, so making them sprites is a persistence problem, not a drawing hook. Hook every routine that writes a cell (a full-tile writer the prototype missed caused 16 stale records), keep a shadow map of cell contents, derive what is on screen from the scroll position at render start, and verify the model against the original screen. Cached item lists go stale through unhooked writers (a bonus scene cycled inks through a third attribute-buffer writer).

lessons.title: Another session can switch a shared git checkout; commit from your own worktree
lessons.text: Two sessions working in the same specnext checkout caused a commit to land on the other session's branch, and a nexclash clone was briefly switched to main under a running task. Using a separate git worktree per task kept uncommitted edits in the owner's checkout untouched. Before committing, confirm which branch is checked out; if a commit lands wrong, rebuild it on the right branch and remove it from the other without disturbing that branch's uncommitted files.

lessons.title: Editing a shared toolkit file marks every game for re-verification
lessons.text: nexclash.py is a dependency of every verification stamp, so editing it would mark all 80 games for re-verification; selftest over all games re-verifies about 60 games in an emulator and takes hours. Prefer additive modules and run targeted checks (a game's own selftest, colour-sheet checks) while developing.

lessons.title: Colour maps keyed by source address mis-colour actors that share graphics
lessons.text: Actors can share source bytes: Gunfright's sheriff and bandits share bodies and legs (a badge painted on one appears on the other) and opponents reuse strip addresses, so one source map lost 48 conflicting colours; the fix is actor-specific identity (IX actor type) with per-actor maps. Heartland's record frame number is not what is in the shift buffer at the plot, so key colours to the bytes drawn and name figures from which record plots them, not from looks. Herbert's painted cache must check source identity as well as raw bytes. Label synthetic fixtures that force a role no recording reaches.

lessons.title: Colour sheet design rules stated by the owner: stable IDs, related sprites adjacent, original colours until painted
lessons.text: For R-Type the owner wants two sheet types (identification with IDs, and painting), with painting sheets laid out like the identification sheets and related sprites (a ship, its shots, its variants) close together; painting sheets carry no text. Figures get stable IDs from what they are (graphic address, size, flips), so regenerating from a longer recording keeps IDs and names, with families that share artwork set once. Figures keep the game's original colours until the owner paints and imports a sheet, and layer order and outline choices should be settable after the build without a rebuild.

lessons.title: Get one live sprite onto the real machine before caches and optimisation
lessons.text: On Inferno the sprites were built last, and once they existed progress was fastest (first visible sprite build, then the full game from tape on a real Next about 7 hours later). Show one sprite in a real .nex first, before caches, loaders or optimisation work.

lessons.title: Opt-in C frame callbacks make previews fast
lessons.text: nexclash.simrun's opt-in C frame callbacks avoid tracing: a 300-frame preview stayed identical while profiling dropped from 19.238 s to 0.724 s, with autosave/buffer parity tested (Inferno).

lessons.title: Simulator T counts omit 28 MHz wait states, contention, DMA and Layer 2 display; JNext adds roughly 1.4x and line-clock reads cost far more
lessons.text: The SkoolKit-based simulator times plain Z80 instructions only (Z80N timings follow the core's VHDL). JNext ran Castle Master's renderer at 1.34-1.42x the simulator's T (wait states), so a worst outdoor view reported as meeting 12.5 fps came to about 10 fps: budget from T x 1.4, report simulator timings as such and re-measure in JNext or on hardware before claiming a frame rate. Flying Shark's handler measured 140,000 T in the simulator against 131,000 in JNext, so the toolkit frame length needed 72,000 T to give the 2-frame beat. Reading the line clock (NextReg $1E/$1F) in a paced update cost far more in JNext than the simulator models (Cisco Heat: 1.2% against 0.2% for four reads an update), so keep it out of paced code and use a counted cost calibrated in JNext; the simulator also undercounted the car-sprite work, so one allowance had to be tuned to JNext (check on real hardware).

lessons.title: Find hook sites by bytes, and check what does not move
lessons.text: The same plotter as a published game's is found by its bytes with addresses left out and the hooks then move address by address (Pssst); AGD builds differ in addresses between games (That Sinking Feeling); byte patterns for site search go through re.escape since 0x2A, 0x28 and 0x5B are regex syntax (Simpsons). What does not move is the game round it: which objects are drawn once, which handlers call the plot's parts. An address map matches code that follows, not code inserted: check every 'after the call' address is call site + 3 in the new game (Stormbringer: a return address landed 7 bytes late).

lessons.title: SkoolKit Snapshot memory for a .z80 has zeros in 0x0000-0x3FFF
lessons.text: Snapshot.get(...).memory[0:0x4000] is all zeros for .z80 files; take ROM bytes from skoolkit.ROM48. Spellbound Dizzy's first hardware build used a ROM-copy page made from the zeros: the font was blank and dialogue boxes were empty. Verify any ROM copy against ROM48 at every ROM byte the game reads. Also snap.ram() is a 48K view even for a 128K snapshot (test snap.machine).

lessons.title: SkoolKit simulator quirks that bite engines and verifiers: it silently drops writes below 0x4000, caches bank pointers, runs one LDIR iteration per execution
lessons.text: The simulator has '> 0x3FFF' guards on writes, so a game or hook that writes into 0x0000-0x3FFF looks fine in simulation (a speed latch in the slot-0 hook page read back 0 in Treasure Island Dizzy) but on the Next a RAM page mapped there, or the alt ROM in write mode, takes the writes (Prince of the Yolkfolk, Spellbound Dizzy). To check, run a simulator copy with the guards removed (Dizzy 6: _rw_simulator()); boot simulation of an alt-ROM copy also needs the guards removed. Replacing Memory.roms after the CSimulator is built does nothing: write the new ROM into the existing buffer in place, or recordings desync on the 48K ROM (Pac-Mania). It caches mapped bank pointers: after restoring a checkpoint outside execution recreate it from the full snapshot, as Memory.out7ffd alone leaves stale mapping. It runs one LDIR iteration per execution, so a model that treats LDIR as one block per call is wrong (Quazatron).

lessons.title: Measurements from builds started at a mid-game snapshot can be invalid
lessons.text: For R-Type, builds started from a snapshot keep sprites off until a life or level restarts, so fallback counts for level 2 taken that way did not count and had to be redone on the full game. Check that the feature under test is actually active in the starting state before trusting a sweep.

lessons.title: Check what state a snapshot was taken in before picking the build target
lessons.text: Atom Ant: the archive's '48K-128K' label is true only of the tape; the 48K .z80 lacks the music block, so check the loader's own paging. Altered Beast: check which banks are zero at intake; a multiload game on a snapshot is one level. Fantasy World Dizzy: a 128K dump saved mid-routine (SP inside the plotter's data) leaves no tail place, so use an alternate dump saved at the title. Gauntlet: block snapshots are taken at the 'rewind tape' prompt, so cut the recording past it. Flying Shark: a loader snapshot holding the game packed takes its sites through a map of the stream's literal bytes.

lessons.title: Builds started from per-level snapshots do not test the tape-start path: test every player path in the delivered form
lessons.text: Inferno's six per-level builds ran on hardware while the tape-start full-game build stalled: the bug sat in the intro phase the snapshots skip, and the real bugs sat at ship death, the menu, restart, multiload and the tape-start intro. Throughout the session nearly every new path (death menu, restart, multiload, tape start) hid at least one bug the simulator missed. Run the whole start path (loader, intro, menu, level load, restart) from the shipped file in JNext or on hardware, not only boot checks and mid-game snapshots.

lessons.title: Startup detection results (Kempston, etc.) are frozen in the snapshot: take it at the title with keyboard controls
lessons.text: R-Type checks for a Kempston interface once at first start and stores the result; the snapshot was taken on a machine without one, so it held 'absent' and ignored the joystick forever in every build made from it. The fix that worked in JNext: clear the stored flag whenever the game reaches its title screens, and force both Next joystick connectors to Kempston mode at start-up because NextZXOS may leave them in another mode (confirmed in the emulator only, not on hardware). The same symptom on Inferno could not be reproduced in JNext and the hardware cause was unconfirmed (a build forcing port 1 to Kempston was made for testing). Conversely a snapshot with the Kempston flag set causes phantom input (Fantasy World Dizzy: byte 62569 = 255 produced phantom input in the recorder), so take the snapshot at the title screen with keyboard controls; a snapshot taken at an odd moment can crash a plain build (Trueno's first snapshot had interrupts off with PC at 0xEEEE: take one from the recording, e.g. rzxplay --stop N), and if it already shows a screen (title or menu) a patch to the drawing code does not show the first time, so patch the snapshot's screen memory too.

lessons.title: A snapshot taken during loading, in BASIC or on a loader screen is not proof of a running loader or game state
lessons.text: Check what a snapshot really is: a (128K) dump may be a BASIC loader while its twin is the game already running (Eagle's Nest); PC 0051 is a captured interrupt, not loader evidence (Head Over Heels); retained BASIC or RAM return does not establish a running loader (Inferno snapinfo); Heartland's snapshot is the tape's BASIC start and the game moves itself down 0x6AC before running, so sites are patched at the snapshot address and verified at their in-play address; Martianoids resumes BASIC before USR, so test the actual startup; a loader's final JP is a stronger entry boundary than a convenient menu PC (Highway Encounter). A 128K snapshot paused in BASIC waits in a PAUSE whose statement returns through the 0x5B00 ROM-swap code and ROM 0, so step to its USR with a key held or start at the USR address with interrupts off (Pac-Mania, Three Weeks: the .nex starts there and 39 bytes go in SIT1); check PC, the stack and PROG before believing 'needs ROM'. Four of Pssst's TOSEC snapshots are stopped on the loading screen and only the [a] ones are at the menu. A snapshot taken in a BASIC loader (PAUSE before USR, code relocated by LDIR) shows only an inert source copy of the engine that byte patterns also match (Spellbound Dizzy): require evidence the copy is live (the ISR or a caller jumps into it) and pre-run the recording to the first frame where the engine is live, finishing any LDIR but stopping BEFORE hardware detection (Kempston check) so it runs live; whole-recording analysis results (low-water, ROM use, printer buffer) are meaningless for such snapshots, so use per-byte first-access data for the game phase.

lessons.title: Compare sound by ordered port FE values and edge timestamps, not event counts
lessons.text: Dizzy Ultimate: compare ordered FE values at matched updates and periods at the same OUT; port counts per wall second mix pace with pitch. Exolon: identical FE values and original CPU speed do not prove pitch, compare edge timestamps; entry video phase alone moves unchanged noise pulses by about +/-107 us, so compare against that control; a median error near 2.6% still hid 14.7% outliers. Cobra: the beeper plays only while waiting for the interrupt.

lessons.title: Running game code at 28 MHz can change audible sound
lessons.text: Atic Atac: check a window for sound first; A403 only queues the room's sound, so the window can end there. The first pass may beep, so it uses catch-up at 7 MHz with the sound routines' first bytes swapped while it is on.

lessons.title: Routines that use SP as a data pointer break stack-based assumptions
lessons.text: A loop using SP as a data pointer yields without CALL, so a coroutine must save SP and live registers (Inferno). A mid-blit snapshot with SP as graphics pointer needs a bounded native prelude (Movie), and an eraser that uses SP as a pointer makes stack low-water measurement unreliable (Magicland Dizzy).

lessons.title: Spec256 .256 images are eight bitplanes followed by the original byte
lessons.text: Exolon: each .256 address holds eight bitplanes then its original byte, not eight palette indices; decode the planes.

lessons.title: Speed latch use: one latch per window, cost counts as game time without frame sync, and exits must restore the caller's speed
lessons.text: Dizzy Ultimate: a short hook can run inside a plotter's 28 MHz window, so use a latch per window (three there); in a game with no frame sync the latch's own time is game time (HLIB_SPEED_IN after the stack switch cost 1.6% with 15 hook calls an update), so read NR 7 first without the stack (51 T) and hook a whole small routine. Commando: with a full alt ROM call one latch routine pair instead of macros inline (25 bytes against 38 for two sites). Finders Keepers: every hook left NR 7 at 3.5 MHz until HK_IN kept the caller's speed on the stack; Cyclone: the verifier logged the latch's IN as a port access, but a NextREG read belongs to the NextREG model. Plot-loop exits that keep no stack and no flags restore speed through a byte of a state page before unmapping it (Midnight Resistance); a hook whose state page is mapped only inside it must map, latch and map again at an exit where other pages were mapped (Incredible Shrinking Fireman); a stateless alt-ROM hook keeps the caller's speed on the stack, 13 bytes more than a fixed exit (Jetpac). Alt ROM space is finite (Jetpac had 1 byte left; Lunar Jetman moved state-page-only code to RAM, keeping the ROM at 914 bytes): check the size after every assemble.

lessons.title: Keep track of whose clock the speed latch holds
lessons.text: If the game can leave its logic without passing the hook that ends it (game over in Silkworm), the next latch reads the build's own 28 MHz as the game's clock for good (interrupts 35 a second, AY writes doubled, updates 60% short); a flag saying whose clock it is fixed it, and only a soak with a seed reaching game over showed it. An ISR hook that sets the speed for the ISR body must put the interrupted speed back (Quazatron: otherwise the rest of a 28 MHz hook ran at 3.5 MHz, fast build 21% slower). Bodies meant to run 'at the original cost' must run at the latched speed, not a fixed 3.5 MHz (Smash TV).

lessons.title: Calibrate the CPU speed-switch cost on the machine instead of assuming the simulator's figure
lessons.text: Timing constants for 28 MHz code that include the cost of switching CPU speed depend on the simulator charging that switch at 3.5 MHz. In Inferno's model, if the real switch is fast and no correction is applied, the paced entry point lands about 230 T early; a one-time measurement at the first window (costing about 1 ms once) corrects it. This was shown in the model only, not on hardware.

lessons.title: If game time follows update duration or loop passes, not wall time, speeding the code speeds the game: hold each update to its original length
lessons.text: In Cisco Heat, drawing sprites with Z80N instructions made a whole update about 21% shorter and the game then ran 14% fast because its speed is set from update duration; the engine adds the saved time back, and builds differing by under 1% should be compared per update on two input seeds (one seed's spread hid a 1.2% loss). Hard Drivin' waits on nothing: each update (car logic, 3D draw, lap clock, copy) takes 7-21 frames and the lap clock counts 5 updates per second, so running everything at 28 MHz would make the game up to 8 times faster; the 3D draw was 87% of the update, so most freed time goes to extra views. Elite (wireframe, back buffer) moves ships a fixed step per main-loop pass (9.7-10.5 frames per update, about 5 updates a second), so it would play several times faster at 28 MHz; the CSpect build waits until 10 frames have passed since the last frame (measured gap exactly 10) and runs the keyboard/sound routine on 16 of every 25 frames to match how often the original accepted interrupts (the original reads controls only about two frames in three; ignoring this made turning about 1.5 times faster). Trap Door showed 0 interrupts accepted in 189,333 frames while its snapshot sat inside the ROM interrupt handler (disassembly confirmed interrupts off and no frame sync): CPU time sets the pace, so every T-state a hook adds changes game speed and hooks must be padded to the original's time; the survey counts do not say this on their own.

lessons.title: Spread sprite-pattern conversion bursts over several updates and fall back to the original drawing meanwhile
lessons.text: R-Type level 3 hiccups were bursts of pattern conversion (pattern store restarts, or the big ship first appearing). Spreading conversion over several updates, drawing unconverted figures the original way meanwhile and backing off pattern-store restarts when the scene cannot fit brought level 3 back to 3 frames per update for 299 of 301 updates, as in the control build; the same scene peaks near 104 of 128 sprites. Computing each cell's colours once instead of per pixel row also sped the converter up.

lessons.title: Black handling in masks: fill enclosed black, keep outside black see-through, and do not let a 1-pixel channel leak
lessons.text: For R-Type sprites, black ink that a 4-connected flood cannot reach from the figure's outside edge is made opaque at build time, as are see-through gaps of up to 2 pixels; black touching the outside stays transparent; an unknown figure falls back to the see-through rule (and should be logged) and the registry can mark a family see-through. R-Type's scenery masks likewise flood black from open sky, 4-connected, over the whole drawn level; black gaps of 1 to 2 pixels between scenery parts are walls and stay solid; masks are stored per distinct cell with a majority vote (a block-local flood was rejected because a black area closed by the next block would turn see-through; a table lookup at draw time replaced a runtime flood that was too slow). Inferno's rule 'black is solid only if fully enclosed' made black see-through whenever it touched the sprite's outside even through a 1-pixel channel, so building window grids, a statue robe and parts of ships leaked the sprite behind; the owner chose G3: black becomes see-through only where a gap at least 3x3 reaches the outside, keeping the old rule for explosions so they stay speckled (seen in JNext on one level-1 scene only; loading takes a few seconds longer, worst level about 9 s against 6.9 s in the simulator).

lessons.title: Set the sprite from the committed state, not a routine's proposed fields
lessons.text: 3D Stock Car: a sprite set from a routine's proposed fields sat off the car after a refused move; set it after the commit, from what the game drew from.

lessons.title: Sprite order and layer order: higher sprite number on top; layer order is global
lessons.text: NextReg $15 bit 6 = 0 (reset) draws the HIGHER sprite number on top, so give objects that must sit behind others the lower numbers (Rainbow: items first, figures after). Layer order is global ($15 bits 4:2): sprites cannot be behind some ULA objects and in front of others. Documentation guarantees at least 100 unscaled 16x16 sprites per line (overflow sets bit 1 of port 0x303B), 128 sprites in total (Rainbow saw 116). A Layer 2 palette priority bit (bit 7 of the second byte) puts chosen Layer 2 pixels above sprites, which gives pixel-exact foreground such as bushes; the palette must then be written through a bank because LAYER PALETTE takes 9 bits.

lessons.title: A sprite outline cannot be hidden by palette tricks; 'off' means leaving the pixels out
lessons.text: Next sprite transparency works on pattern index 0, not on a palette colour. An outline option that turns the outline off therefore has to leave the outline pixels out of the sprite images. In Lunar Jetman the rover's outline and fill share index 8, so a palette change cannot separate them. Changing only the outline colour (for example to black) is a palette-only change and is cheap: Renegade needed 32 palette bytes, but forcing white on all four levels differed from its default because level 2 was already black.

lessons.title: A border inside the figure's own 8x8 cells cannot outline a figure that fills its cells; pre-render a ring one pixel bigger
lessons.text: The owner chose an optional 4-neighbour border (clear pixel touching a visible pixel up, down, left or right, no diagonals), settable per figure. Done through colour pages it stays inside the figure's cells: on R-Type's player ship, which fills its cells top to bottom, it gave no top or bottom border and filled gaps in the dotted pattern that open onto the cell edge, making the ship look solid. A proper ring needs each marked graphic pre-rendered one pixel bigger on every side as ready-made sprite patterns, placed one pixel up and left (mirroring still lines up; 24x8 became 26x10 and still fitted two sprites; pacing unchanged, 297 of 301 updates at 3 frames); a black border only shows where the figure crosses other sprites or stars, a hit flash drops the border, and hand-painted pixels override the automatic border.

lessons.title: 4-bit sprite programming facts that hardware runs confirmed
lessons.text: 4-bit anchor sprite attr4: 0x80 = pattern-slot bytes 0-127, 0xC0 = bytes 128-255 (the guide's relative-sprite table reads the other way). Pattern upload: port 0x303B selects the slot (bit 7 = +128 bytes), 256-byte uploads to 0x5B auto-advance; a 4-bit pattern whose rows 8-15 are empty can be done with zeroed pattern RAM and 64 bytes per sprite. NextReg $35-$39 set one attribute of the sprite selected by $34 ($38 = 0 hides); $4B defaults to E3, set 0 for 4-bit transparency; $43 = 0x20 edits sprite palette 0 with auto-increment ($40 index, $41 RRRGGGBB); $19 clip needs the index reset via $1C bit 1, then X1, X2, Y1, Y2.

lessons.title: Attribute NextRegs and port 0x57 use separate sprite selectors; models must not alias them
lessons.text: Attribute NextRegs and port 57 use separate sprite selectors; a simulator that aliases them falsely approves stale copies (Herbert; explicit port selection and a broken-selector negative now cover it). In Heartland, hooklib.NextModel let NextReg 0x34 set the attribute port's sprite, which the machine does only with lockstep on: a build relying on it passed every check and showed echoes within the owner's first minute.

lessons.title: Reuse a built sprite store when the same level restarts, keyed on the level, and keep per-start state resettable
lessons.text: Inferno's sprite driver rebuilt every sprite at each play start. Remembering the last built level (from the level digit) and skipping the rebuild when it matches cut the wait from 410 frames to 0 in JNext on a retry, while a different level still did a full rebuild. The driver's reset routine was split into a soft part run on every start (display and sprite-slot state) and an index reset for full builds only. A test harness that starts with the store empty always does a full build.

lessons.title: Distinguish the 128-pattern limit from upload speed; faster uploads cannot fix a scene that needs more patterns at once
lessons.text: R-Type's level 3 battleship hull needed about 180 patterns on screen at once because each strip became up to 7 sprites and patterns. Ideas that only change how patterns reach the 128 slots (DMA re-arm uploads, a Next RAM store of converted patterns, reference-counted slots, copper commits) make churn cheaper but cannot raise the on-screen limit; copper multiplexing raises the sprite count, not the pattern count. For R-Type conversion cost, not the 128-byte OTIR upload, was the expensive part. Count patterns needed per update before choosing a fix.

lessons.title: PUSH fills with interrupts on: the ISR must use its own stack
lessons.text: Filling Layer 2 spans of 16 pixels or more with PUSH (5.5 T per pixel instead of 11) runs with interrupts on while the stack points into the screen bank. The interrupt entry must switch to its own stack before using more than its 2-byte return address. A sweep imitating that write at 75,666 random moments left every picture correct. The clear of dithered sky/ground rows used the same fill.

lessons.title: Do not change live sprites piece by piece while the game draws; stage and commit in one burst
lessons.text: Changing sprite patterns and attributes during Rainbow's render showed tearing and ghosting (a new pattern appeared at the old position until its attributes followed). Fix: stage attributes and pattern sources during the render and commit them sprite by sprite (pattern, then attributes) at render end, then hide the rest; about 1.6k T per sprite at 28 MHz, 84 sprites ~5 ms. Verify pixels against the staged state and the commit against the staged data.

lessons.title: Hooks that keep no state need no RAM page and may run with interrupts on
lessons.text: Chuckie Egg's hooks live in the alt ROM, use the game's own stack for scratch and write output only through NEXTREG, so no page is mapped and interrupts stay enabled (an interrupt between two NEXTREGs is harmless). It fits when the game's ISR does not touch the sprite registers being written. Not yet confirmed on hardware in the notes.

lessons.title: The survey is slow on long recordings: run a short first look, reuse stored results and expect gaps
lessons.text: On a 189,333-frame (63 minute) recording (Trap Door) the survey took 64 minutes where the checklist asks for 3 to 5 minutes of play (the playbook's guide is about 5 minutes per 8,600 frames); a first look with --stop 15000 would have answered the same questions, and every scan command (for example --writers) replays the recording again. A repeat run with identical snapshot, recordings and arguments can return the stored result in 0.1 s (--fresh to rerun) and a warning exists for long recordings; the survey can name the rendering model, copier source buffer and pacing itself instead of leaving it to disassembly. survey --full failed on a loader snapshot (Dizzy 5), which auto handles itself, so that game cannot enter the research database by that route.

lessons.title: Survey 'Findings' lines are heuristics from counts, not verified classifications
lessons.text: The rendering-model line in the survey Findings comes from counts (writers, block copies, buffers). Across 28 seeded entries: 7 back buffer, 15 several routines draw directly, 4 one routine draws most pixels, 1 cell copier, 1 unclassified (Knight Tyme, 128K). Seeded fingerprints come only from the first 3,000 frames of one recording, and no cross-game fingerprint match had been observed yet; the matcher was proven only on a synthetic relocated routine.

lessons.title: survey --full cannot replay a loader snapshot; auto handles the loader itself
lessons.text: For Spellbound Dizzy (Dizzy 5) the survey warns that the snapshot is a loader snapshot and to run the loader first, yet `auto` builds it and handles the loader itself (verified: 1,479 plots pixel-perfect, 1,463 erases). `survey --full` fails there ('port reading(s) left for frame 421') because the plain-conversion analysis cannot replay a loader snapshot, so such a game gets no research-database entry.

lessons.title: The survey's routine table can miss plotters that a pixel-versus-sprite comparison finds
lessons.text: Green Beret: the survey missed the mine plotter and the small plotter's order; comparing original pixels with sprites, by frame, found both.

lessons.title: A survey of an idle menu or stopped game finds only the idle drawing
lessons.text: The first Winter Sports Downhill survey saw only the speed bars because the free run never started a descent; the descent began only when the first defined control key was held. Script the key sequence that really starts play before surveying, and check the survey sees the figure drawing.

lessons.title: Survey preview sheets are tinted per routine; do not read the tint as game colour
lessons.text: A survey preview of Elite looked coloured (orange or cyan viewports, purple scanner) and was first misread as the game's real colour; the viewport is white on black. The survey writer was changed to say the preview sheet is tinted per routine. Check a plain screenshot of the real snapshot before drawing colour conclusions.

lessons.title: A survey row with more T per call than a frame is probably the main loop
lessons.text: The shadow call stack can attribute the main loop to a routine: on Trap Door a routine 'called from top' showed a maximum of 21,457,175 T per call, which is the main loop, not a drawing routine. Treat rows whose T per call exceeds a frame as suspect.

lessons.title: A start-up tail at 0xC000 or above vanishes when its own 7FFD write remaps the top 16K
lessons.text: The converter stub runs from its own bank at 0xC000-0xFFFF and the tail's OUT to 7FFD maps the game's bank 0 back there, so a tail placed at 0xC000+ disappears from under the PC. This applies to 48K games too, not only 128K: El Capitan Trueno's plain .nex crashed at once because the tail was put below SP at 0xFF97 (its printer buffer was in use); the toolkit's own boot simulation (nextboot.check) showed it, but the plain build did not run it. Fix: pick a tail site proven write-first by an access scan over the recording (Trueno: 0xA6C9) and run the boot check on plain builds as well.

lessons.title: A bank loader standing in for tape must rewind and must not lose its block list
lessons.text: Inferno's restart after death requests an earlier level's data by name, so a bank loader that reads blocks strictly in order must wrap to the first block past the end; snapshots start partway through the tape and hide this. The real cause of the hang on the loading screen was the driver build copying a near-empty page over the page holding the tape block list, so the loader saw zero blocks; the wrap was worth having but was not the fix. Make the build fail its check when the block list is empty.

lessons.title: Tape and loader intake: slow tap2sna, compressed screens, encoded loaders, multiloads
lessons.text: Atom Ant: tap2sna hit its 200-second limit on a loaded machine and needs `--press 7:ENTER` for the tape's PAUSE. Exolon: the TAP screen is compressed; execute its original decoder (8001, from the sixth block) rather than looking for a 6914-byte block. Bubbler: the archive loader complements 37,300 bytes before entry, so compare a decoded execution state, not the encoded loader RAM. Gauntlet: one recording that holds a real tape load fixes a multiload layout and the rest compare with the tape file; Cisco Heat took 61,044 bytes from the tape with --tape-bank and carried 3,096.

lessons.title: Offer a test cheat early and remove it at the end; pixel art is the human's job
lessons.text: Process rules agreed on Trueno: ask whether the game has pause, menus or message windows over the play area; offer to find an immortality cheat at the start to test a long game and switch it off at the end, then check the game-over path; the AI can only copy cells as they are, so offer the human a sheet to redraw scenery clash cells or figures. For a long game fix many items per emulator pass, because the places are far apart.

lessons.title: Do not edit the tree while a selftest or compare runs; look at the picture before trusting a number
lessons.text: A selftest's stamp hashes the tree at its start, so no edits while it runs (Three Weeks, full verify about 45 min detached). R-Type's compare tool rebuilds each level from the current files, so a half-edited layout gave a false 'huge slowdown' on levels 2-8, cleared by a worktree bisect and a needless bisect. Never run two CSpect jobs at once, and look at a picture before trusting a count: several R-Type measuring scripts counted the wrong thing (stars as sprites, magenta stars as the power-up carrier, a crop that missed the letters).

lessons.title: Test a claim about the fix-off path before writing it
lessons.text: A note said the fix line off scrambles the picture, but the real loader showed the OS loader runs the original correctly (Mad Mix 2). Test a claim about the off path before documenting it.

lessons.title: Patch compressed game text in RAM just after each block unpacks instead of recompressing
lessons.text: Inferno's text is compressed on tape in the main code and in each level block. Once decompressed it is plain text with control codes, so the English build overwrites it in RAM just after each block unpacks, driven by a table of (count, destination, bytes). This avoids recompressing and tape checksums. Longer strings can borrow space from short neighbours by repacking a block and updating its pointers. Picture-based text needs different handling: only the white-on-blue text cells of story screens were replaced, leaving the title picture.

lessons.title: A huge slow figure drawn outside the plotters can live on a 1-bit tilemap instead of sprites
lessons.text: R-Type's level 3 battleship (46 x 13 cells, 333 non-empty, 326 distinct, about 180 sprite patterns, overflowing the pattern memory) was moved to a text-mode tilemap: 1-bit tiles at 8 bytes each (326 tiles is 2.6 KB, needing 512-tile mode, map 2.5 KB) keep the original's two colours per cell where a 4-bit version (10.4 KB) would not fit. Tilemap tile data and map must sit in bank 5 or the lower 8K of bank 7; bank 7's lower 8K held packed level data, so on a 2 MB Next it is copied to a spare page when the ship appears and restored on every screen change and before any level unpack (shared with the packed level data; drawn every 8th update in whole-cell moves). Result on level 3: fallback moments 387 to 8, sprites in use at once 119 to 69, gameplay unchanged; motion is two scroll register writes, which can also glide the figure.

lessons.title: Make the ULA pane's paper colour transparent to show a Layer 2 backdrop behind game-drawn lines
lessons.text: For Winter Sports Downhill the left pane's white background was made see-through so a Layer 2 panorama scrolled by the hardware scroll register showed behind the black poles the game still draws on the ULA. It worked on a real Next, and the game state matched the plain build frame for frame. The risk checked was a stray white block where transparency fails.

lessons.title: The ULA reads bank 5 directly; remapping slots 2/3 changes only the CPU view
lessons.text: A canvas page mapped over 0x4000-0x7FFF is invisible to the ULA, which is why Rainbow could re-run original plotters into a private canvas page. The ULA picture changes only when bank 5 itself is written.

lessons.title: Drive branches that recordings never reach with unit cases from captured state
lessons.text: When no recording reaches a branch, drive it directly: Jetpac's free run never built the rocket, so unit tests ran the game's own routines from a captured state with the rocket's fields poked (a guard derived from a name, part < 3, was wrong because 3 meant fuel). Heartland's unit case forcing each way of the attribute copy found an R fault the recordings, which take only the plain path, could not. One object drawing four figures a frame, with the same IX, defeats a sprite set per object and passes a per-draw check that compares each draw alone (Jetpac, Lunar Jetman).

lessons.title: Design rule: hide waits the conversion adds and keep the original game's flow and speed
lessons.text: The project owner stated, for Inferno, that a delay the Next conversion adds (sprite build after the story screen, on every retry) should be hidden or removed, not accepted, and that the original game's behaviour should be kept where possible: keep the menu and typing, remove only the added step. Cheap measures preferred: continue the loader-style border bars through the wait, or skip the rebuild when nothing changed. For Cisco Heat the loading screen was wanted to appear at once, hold about 4 seconds or until a key, and have no hold in the NXC build.

lessons.title: The verifier must model NextREG ports and carry Next state between hooks
lessons.text: A verifier that feeds every port read from the recording fails on the speed latch's IN 0x253B: answer it from a NextREG model (Spellbound, Target Renegade; 'port access in a hook' is a model matter). A model rebuilt for every hook run forgets where the pattern and attribute ports stood, so a build that never selected the attribute port's sprite passed until the model carried both between hooks (Simpsons). An old verifier ran NEXTREG in 0 T while z80n.install counts 20/17 T, which pace accounting needs (Solomon's Key).

lessons.title: Running a ROM-dependent game over NextZXOS's ROM3 versus a whole alt ROM image
lessons.text: A whole Sinclair alt ROM image can make a key-wait stub unnecessary (Cobra) and lets the TOSEC BASIC run to its USR call as on a 48K (Dynamite Dan), proven by the ROM path check. A partial alt ROM whose rest is NextZXOS's ROM3 runs ROM code as NextZXOS's on hardware (Cauldron: menu hung, keys dead), and Chuckie Egg's pinned build over ROM3 reads 89 ROM data bytes that differ (a whole image shows none; simulation only). Atom Ant over ROM3 differed in 5 to 10 ROM bytes of the 128K ROM with no game difference in JNext lockstep.

lessons.title: Short or partial runs miss rare paths: replay whole recordings
lessons.text: The first 1,500 frames passed everything in Olli and Lissa; the whole second recording found four faults (a line-lower draw from y=169, a wipe with interrupts on, a one-off pose, a later room's data under the tail). Simpsons' clip rows were found only by whole recordings (3 of 5 levels); Nemesis: 2000 frames missed two cases that 20000 found; Pssst's replay stopped at 6,000 of 20,000 frames from a default meant for free runs. Treat 'static graphics' as provisional until every recording has passed (Pac-Mania's second writer showed after six recordings). Replay a recording to its end and pick the tail address from every recording.

lessons.title: Iterate checks cheaply: rerun failing states, then a spread-out sample, then one full run per commit
lessons.text: On Inferno a full six-level state check took about 18-25 minutes and rare failures (2-4 of 1,855 states, 0.2%) are missed by a sample, and repeated full runs during debugging were wasted. What worked: rerun only the known failing states first (about 25 seconds, via a per-state selector), then a spread-out sample (every 10th state, about 2 minutes) to catch systematic bias, and exactly one full run as the gate before each commit; one process per level cut the full run from about 18 minutes to about 5. Each state's cases depend only on its level and index, so a subset checks exactly what the full run checks.

lessons.title: Windows CRLF line endings: false doc-budget overruns, stale stamps and failing checks
lessons.text: On Windows, git autocrlf and Python write CRLF, which adds a byte per line: doccheck's byte budgets (for example 25,000 bytes for a game note) then report false overruns (18 failures on one clone, Inferno notes about 24.5-24.8 KB, a clean main failing), while an LF checkout passes and the Linux CI result is the one that counts; fix the tool to count LF bytes rather than trimming files repeatedly, and do not commit a CRLF-only edit that makes git show a whole file as changed (Alien 8, R-Type notes). Record stamps fingerprint files byte for byte, so profile, record and generated-view files written with CRLF made the stamp stale until converted back to LF, and a stamped selftest had to be re-run after line-ending normalisation (Rainbow Z80N); normalise generated files to LF before stamping or committing. With core.autocrlf=true the workflow tests' temporary repos turned .gitignore into CRLF and failed with a baseline conflict (setting core.autocrlf false in the three temporary-repo setups fixed it), the selftest planner treats some games' files as changed because line endings change their hashes, and records views writes CRLF; run checks from an LF-only copy. Backslash paths broke a doccheck budget lookup and sjasmplus wanted forward slashes; fresh clones may have no git user name or email, which makes commits fail until set repo-locally. Doccheck also requires Lessons, Technique use and Friction sections in a game note.

lessons.title: Python and shell pitfalls: a scratch file named dis.py shadows the stdlib; heredocs lose backslashes; stale shared modules
lessons.text: A helper or scratch file named dis.py in the working folder shadows the stdlib dis and breaks SkoolKit (circular import) and PIL's PNG import (Mad Mix 2; three times in Castle Master). Python written through a shell heredoc loses its backslash escapes (Castle Master, Cisco Heat): write a file with the Write tool. A module restored from an older copy can silently drop another engine's hook (identify() lost the Dizzy V dispatch, and dizzy5 analysis stopped resyncing per segment), so run the selftest after any session that touches shared modules and rebuild known MD5s first when files were transcribed by hand; an uploaded snapshot with a different MD5 may be another snapshot of the same game. A C-simulator run without interrupts never returns from a wait loop; JNext screenshot names count from the start line while log F counts from power-on (500 apart); auto takes one --rzx per recording (Crystal Kingdom Dizzy).

lessons.title: On Windows check that the pinned assembler and zx0 packer exist before trusting selftest
lessons.text: The pinned sjasmplus ships only for Linux; a local Windows sjasmplus 1.24.0 was used after confirming it reproduced every other engine's hook bytes exactly. There was no C compiler, and nxcout only finds the compressor as a file named zx0 with no extension: a zx0 binary from upstream's pinned Windows build worked after its SHA-256 matched the pin and it reproduced the repo's pinned test output exactly. Without zx0, 17 of the 20 selftest --tools failures were .nxc tests, so those failures were environmental, not regressions; running selftest on a machine that cannot prove push access needed the maintainer environment flag. A patch menu allows at most 4 toggles, cheats come from .pok files (none means no cheats; 80 of 84 existing patches had some), and a built patch is checked by reproducing the sprite build byte for byte (one patch carried an English/Czech toggle and reproduced both builds).

lessons.title: Elite-style wireframe: buffer cleared every frame and lines ORed, so per-object colour needs no ownership map
lessons.text: Probing Elite showed the game clears the whole viewport buffer each frame with one block copy and then ORs lines in, never erasing by XOR; where lines cross, the one drawn last can set the colour. Each ship is drawn by one routine during which IY holds that ship's blueprint address (11 models seen), so colouring by object type is possible; planet, stars, text and lasers each come from separate routines. Re-running the ship draw to interpolate must save and restore a ship flags byte the draw changes and the logic later reads.

lessons.title: Ranking screen writers or a rounded buffer range can point at the copier or at renderer variables
lessons.text: Bubbler: masked actors and scenery compose into a 24-byte stride buffer and a stack copier publishes it, but ranking screen writers initially emphasised the copier and menus. Castle Master: the survey's buffer range (0x5C80-0x673F, rounded) mixed the view buffer with renderer variables so `scan --writers` listed geometry code first; the copier's own pointer (LD HL,23740 at 0xA39A) gave the exact buffer.

lessons.title: An empty screen is a wrong reference for an XOR plotter that draws the frame it erases
lessons.text: On an empty screen an XOR plotter draws the frame it means to erase, so the empty screen is a reference only for an entry that draws and erases nothing; elsewhere use a model of the figure and check the draw-only entries against that model. In Cookie this check found what the model missed: the game draws nothing for a figure whose bottom line is above line 31 (a signed compare in the cut).

lessons.title: XOR plotters: visibility is draw parity and an overlay toggled on every call needs no place list, but parity does not always mean on screen
lessons.text: A game that XORs figures needs no place list: toggling the overlay on every call keeps it exact through erase, draw and redraw (Page Pharaoh, Spellbound: an erase names the place it is already); on Layer 2, XOR on eight planes equals XOR on the value when the buffer holds the set's own 8-bit values, so no masks are needed (Page Pharaoh; test a named risk before designing round it). A pure XOR plotter with no undo buffer (Dizzy 1) needs visibility modelled as the parity of draws and erases (7 double draws cancel on screen), and a plotter's return registers can differ when the figure is not on screen (A after erase in Dizzy 1): check whether callers use them before 'fixing'. Limit: parity does not mean 'is on screen' because clears, scrolls and text wipe or move XOR figures without an erase (Cauldron frames 2602-2638) and parts that XOR-cancel an image break per-key parity (Atic Atac death: 18 one-row slices, 19 sprites over a blank screen); group by graphic + base line with a row mask and check the group, and without an object table key an overlay by (graphic, x, y, rows, width) and let other writers taint it.

lessons.title: Z80 divide loops: step with the divisor negated and skip zero top bytes
lessons.text: Castle Master's 32-bit divide went from about 1,967 T to about 970 T a call by doing 8 bits at a time with the divisor negated (ADD sets the carry, so no compare) and skipping top bytes that are zero. The same step in the projection divide gave 698 T down to 637 T. The row fill gained by starting a PUSH fill from the row's end whatever its parity (530 T down to 495 T a row).

lessons.title: SkoolKit runs unknown Z80N opcodes as silent NOPs; install and control-test them
lessons.text: For a Z80N opcode used in hooks (Rainbow's SWAPNIB, ED 23) install it in every simulator that runs the hooks, test it exhaustively, and add a control that runs the hooks with it as SkoolKit's silent NOP: that control must fail. NEXTREG (ED 91 / ED 92) is not a SkoolKit opcode either; install handlers in sim.after_ED, with ports via the tracer. Block instructions use per-byte list indexing, so a list subclass can model paging.

lessons.title: DMA auto-restart in continuous mode locks the CPU out
lessons.text: WR5 values A2, AA, B2 or BA (auto-restart) with a continuous-mode memory copy freeze the machine at once, because the transfer restarts as soon as it ends and the CPU never runs. This is normal Z80 DMA behaviour, but the documentation does not warn about it.

lessons.title: zxnDMA blitter commands observed on core 3.03.00
lessons.text: Send these after LOAD (CF) and before ENABLE (87): DF m is a mode byte (bit 1 uses the E3 length, bit 2 transparent copy, bit 3 fill; bits 2+3 together, bit 0 or bit 4 give no transfer; it stays set until RESET C3). F3 c sets the transparent colour (default 0) and F7 v the fill value (default 0), both before DF. E3 lo hi is the length (at least 1). D7, DB, E7, EB and EF are accepted but had no visible effect; no stride mode was found. Only an Issue 2 board was tested, and on port 0x0B the DF modes were inconsistent.

lessons.title: The undocumented DF fill mode with a search-mode WR0 reads I/O ports without a length limit
lessons.text: With a standard program (length 32) followed by 42 DF 08 87, the DMA reads I/O port N and writes it to memory address N upward from the destination, ignoring the programmed length and never stopping; in continuous mode the machine freezes and only a reset helps (burst mode wrote 4,113 bytes in about a second). The same sequence made NextZXOS stop with 'attempted to access the +3 FDC hardware' although the register 0xD8 documentation says the DMA cannot trigger traps; setting 0xD8 to 0 stopped that. Observed on core 3.03.00 / firmware 1.46 only.

lessons.title: A Z80 DMA WR4 byte with 'interrupt control follows' locks the Next DMA until power-off
lessons.text: On an Issue 2 board, core 3.03.00: after a normal memory-to-memory program, writing WR4 byte 91 (D4=1) then 87 left every later transfer failing, including a fresh health-check copy. Six C3 resets, A3, AF, 8B and a rewritten WR4 did not recover it; only switching the machine off did (a hard reset was untested). Only 91 was tested; the other bytes of the form 1xx1xx01 were assumed to behave alike. Do not port Z80 DMA code that sets interrupt control onto the zxnDMA.
